Proposition 1 For any random variable X, we have 
    X = F_X^{-1}(U).



Proof. For any x, we have

 Thus X = F_X^{-1}(U).

title: Inverse Sampling Transform
section: 2 Application: Uniform Sampling on a Disk
text:
2 Application: Uniform Sampling on a Disk
Now, we want to perform uniform sampling on the unit disk. We use polar coordinates; more specifically, we take r\cos(\theta), r\sin(\theta), where

r \in [0,1] such that P(r) \propto r (\Rightarrow P(r) = 2r)
\theta \sim U(0,2\pi)

The key lies in 1., that is, how to sample r such that P(r) = 2r. Let X be the random variable such that P(X = r) = 2r. Then, F_X(x) = \int_0^x 2r\,dr = x^2, and thus F_X^{-1}(y) = \sqrt{y}.

2.1 Code
With above in mind, we sample 10000 points on the unit disk, see Figure 1.


Code
import numpy as np
import matplotlib.pyplot as plt

# 1. Sample the points
N = 10000
inv_cdf = lambda x: np.sqrt(x)
R = np.vectorize(inv_cdf)(np.random.uniform(0, 1, N))
T = np.random.uniform(0, 2*np.pi, N)
points = [(r * np.cos(t), r * np.sin(t)) for r, t in zip(R, T)]

# 2. Make a scatter plot
x, y = zip(*points)
plt.scatter(x, y, s=1)
plt.xticks([])
plt.yticks([])
ax = plt.gca()
ax.set_aspect('equal')
ax.spines['top'].set_visible(False)
ax.spines['right'].set_visible(False)
ax.spines['bottom'].set_visible(False)
ax.spines['left'].set_visible(False)
plt.show()








Figure 1: Sampling 10000 points uniformly on the unit disk.

section: 1 · Newton’s law: the equation of motion
text:
1 · Newton’s law: the equation of motion
Mathematics used: partial derivatives (explained) and the small-angle approximation.
Apply Newton’s law, mass times acceleration equals force, to one short piece of the string. The only force on the piece comes from the tension pulling at its two ends, and it turns out to depend only on how the string bends there.
1. Set up the string. Let the string run along x from the nut, at x = 0, to the bridge, at x = L. It is stretched with tension T, a pulling force, and has mass \mu per unit length. Write u(x, t) for its height above the straight line at position x and time t. Take the short piece between x and x + dx; its mass is \mu\,dx.
2. The tension pulls each end of the piece along the string. If the string at a point makes a small angle \theta with the straight line, the upward part of the pull is T\sin\theta; for a small angle \sin\theta \approx \tan\theta (both are about \theta in radians), and \tan\theta is the slope. So the upward part of the pull is the tension times the slope. At the right end the rest of the string pulls with upward part T\,u_x(x + dx); at the left end it pulls the other way, with upward part -T\,u_x(x). Here u_x is the slope, the derivative in x with the time held fixed (a partial derivative).

  
  
  
  
  
  TT
  xx + dx
  upward part of each pull ≈ T × slope

3. Add the two pulls. The net upward force on the piece is the difference of the slopes at its two ends, times T: 
T\,u_x(x + dx) - T\,u_x(x) \approx T\,u_{xx}\,dx ,
 where u_{xx}, the rate at which the slope changes, is the string’s curvature. On a hump the slope falls from left to right, u_{xx} < 0, and the net force pulls the piece down.
4. Newton’s law. The piece’s acceleration is u_{tt}, the second derivative of the height in time with x held fixed. Mass times acceleration equals force: \mu\,dx\;u_{tt} = T\,u_{xx}\,dx. Divide by \mu\,dx: 
u_{tt} = c^2\,u_{xx}, \qquad c^2 = \frac{T}{\mu}.
 This is the wave equation; c is the speed at which a bump runs along the string.
What we assumed. Small slopes, so that the tension stays T and its upward part is T times the slope; the same tension and mass per length everywhere; a perfectly flexible string, with no stiffness (a real string is slightly stiff: page 7); no air and no friction; and ends that are held perfectly still.



Step-by-step derivationThe same equation from beads with the ends tied uses matrices, as on page 2

Put N beads of mass m, spaced h apart, on a thread of tension T, with both ends tied, so u_0 = u_{N+1} = 0. The force on bead j is the one derived on the ring page, so m\ddot u_j = \frac{T}{h}(u_{j+1} - 2u_j + u_{j-1}). The matrix is now the ring’s matrix without its two corner entries: 
K = \begin{pmatrix} 2 & -1 & & \\ -1 & 2 & \ddots & \\ & \ddots & \ddots & -1\\ & & -1 & 2 \end{pmatrix}.
 Its eigenvectors are v_j = \sin\big(n\pi j/(N+1)\big), the sampled sines, with eigenvalues 4\sin^2\big(n\pi/(2(N+1))\big) for n = 1, \dots, N. To check: \sin(\alpha(j+1)) + \sin(\alpha(j-1)) = 2\cos\alpha\,\sin(\alpha j), so (Kv)_j = (2 - 2\cos\alpha)\,v_j = 4\sin^2(\alpha/2)\,v_j with \alpha = n\pi/(N+1), and the tied ends hold because \sin 0 = \sin n\pi = 0. As on the ring, letting N \to \infty with L = (N+1)h and \mu = m/h fixed gives the wave equation and the frequencies f_n = \frac{n}{2L}\sqrt{T/\mu} found below.

title: Why does a light touch make a string jump an octave?
text:
2 · The operator
Read the equation of motion as a rule. The acceleration of each point is c^2u_{xx}: take the string’s shape, find its curvature at every point, and multiply by c^2. Minus that, the restoring force per unit mass, is the string’s operator, A = -c^2\,d^2/dx^2, and the equation reads u_{tt} = -Au.
The ends are tied. At the nut and the bridge the string cannot move: u(0, t) = 0 and u(L, t) = 0 at every moment. So A only ever acts on shapes that stay still at both ends. This restriction is a boundary condition, here a Dirichlet condition. An operator is the rule together with the shapes it is allowed to act on, so the tied ends are part of the operator: they decide which shapes are eigenfunctions, and so which frequencies the string has.

The string’s operator. The equation of motion is 
\begin{gathered} u_{tt} = -A\,u, \\ A = -c^2\,\frac{d^2}{dx^2}, \qquad c^2 = \frac{T}{\mu}, \end{gathered}
 acting on shapes X on [0, L] with X(0) = X(L) = 0. In words: A takes a shape and returns minus c^2 times its curvature, and only shapes that stay still at both ends are allowed.

title: Why does a light touch make a string jump an octave?
text:
3 · Its spectrum
A mode is a shape that the operator only rescales: AX = \lambda X. The shape X is an eigenfunction, and the number \lambda its eigenvalue. Released in that shape, the string keeps it and swings at the angular frequency \omega = \sqrt\lambda, that is, at f = \sqrt\lambda/2\pi in hertz. The list of all eigenvalues is the spectrum. Here is the whole computation.
1. Which shapes does the operator only rescale? AX = \lambda X says -c^2X'' = \lambda X. Write \lambda = c^2k^2 with k > 0; then X'' = -k^2X, a shape whose curvature is minus k^2 times itself. Its solutions are the waves X = a\cos kx + b\sin kx. (Zero and negative \lambda give no shape that stays still at both ends; see the first proof fold below.)
2. Hold the nut still. X(0) = 0 forces a = 0, so X = b\sin kx.
3. Hold the bridge still. X(L) = 0 then needs \sin kL = 0, so kL is a whole multiple of \pi: k = n\pi/L for n = 1, 2, 3, \dots The shape \sin(n\pi x/L) has n arches.
4. Turn the eigenvalues into frequencies. The eigenvalues are \lambda_n = c^2k_n^2 = (n\pi c/L)^2, so 
f_n = \frac{\sqrt{\lambda_n}}{2\pi} = \frac{n\,c}{2L} = \frac{n}{2L}\sqrt{\frac{T}{\mu}} = n\,f_1 .


The string’s spectrum. Eigenfunctions: \sin(n\pi x/L), the shapes with n = 1, 2, 3, \dots arches. Eigenvalues: \lambda_n = (n\pi c/L)^2. Frequencies: f_n = n f_1, with 
f_1 = \frac{1}{2L}\sqrt{\frac{T}{\mu}},
 exactly 1, 2, 3, … times the lowest. The lowest rises with the tension and falls with the length and the mass per length.

In plain words: a shape with n arches is n times shorter than the one-arch shape; a shorter shape bends more sharply, and the string pulls back in proportion to how sharply it bends, so it is pulled back n² times harder and swings n times faster. Each arch shape is exactly half of a wave on a loop twice as long, so the string keeps half of the loop’s waves from page 3. One thing does change: on a loop each frequency had two waves, one shifted along the loop; on a string a wave cannot run around, it reflects at the ends, and each frequency has a single shape, a standing wave.



ProofNo other eigenvalues uses integration by parts

Write the eigenvalue as \lambda = c^2 k^2 for some number k^2, so that -X'' = k^2 X. Multiply by X and integrate from 0 to L. Integrating by parts, the boundary term -X X' vanishes at both ends because X = 0 there: 
k^2\int_0^L X^2\,dx = \int_0^L (X')^2\,dx .
 So a zero or negative \lambda would need \int (X')^2\,dx \le 0, which only the constant shapes satisfy, and the only constant that vanishes at the ends is X = 0. Each eigenvalue (n\pi c/L)^2 has multiplicity 1: the boundary condition at the nut removed the cosine.





ProofThe string is half of a circle: the sine series as a Fourier series uses Fourier series and the uniqueness of solutions of the wave equation

Take a shape u on [0, L] with u(0) = u(L) = 0. Extend it to [-L, 0] by u(-x) = -u(x), an odd reflection, and then repeat with period 2L. The result is a shape on a loop of circumference 2L.

  
  
  
  
  0L−L
  stringodd reflection


Odd shapes stay odd. If u(x, t) solves the wave equation on the loop, so does -u(-x, t), since two derivatives in x do not change sign under x \mapsto -x. Starting from an odd shape at rest, both are the same solution by uniqueness, so the motion stays odd.
Odd shapes on the loop are exactly string shapes. An odd periodic shape vanishes at 0, because u(0) = -u(0), and at L, because u(L) = u(-L) = -u(L). Conversely every string shape extends this way.
So the string’s eigenfunctions are the loop’s odd eigenfunctions. On a loop of circumference 2L the eigenfunctions of -c^2\,d^2/dx^2 are \cos(n\pi x/L) and \sin(n\pi x/L), with eigenvalues (n\pi c/L)^2. The odd ones are the sines. Each eigenvalue keeps one of its two eigenfunctions, which is why the multiplicity drops from 2 to 1.

The sine series of a string shape, u = \sum_n b_n\sin(n\pi x/L), is therefore the Fourier series of its odd extension, and everything proved on the circle page carries over: every string shape is a sum of the string’s modes. The same trick with an even reflection, u(-x) = u(x), gives the cosines and the condition u'(0) = u'(L) = 0; the next page combines both reflections for air in a tube.

title: Why does a light touch make a string jump an octave?
text:
5 · What we hear
A light touch keeps only the shapes that are still under the finger. Where a shape has a still point, a node, the finger has nothing to grab, and that shape rings on. Every other shape moves under the finger and loses its energy to it within a moment. The shape \sin(n\pi x/L) is still at the middle exactly when n is even: 2, 4, 6, … arches, at 2, 4, 6, … times the open string’s frequency. The survivors repeat twice as often, so you hear a note an octave up. At a third, the survivors have 3, 6, 9, … arches: three times the frequency, an octave and a fifth up (a factor 2 times a factor 3/2). (In this simple model the finger drains each shape in proportion to how much that shape moves under it, the rule the piano page derives for felt dampers.)



PreciselyWhich modes survive a light touch uses the sine function

Let the finger touch the string at the distance s from the nut, and write X_n(x) = \sin(n\pi x/L) for the shape of mode n. In the model, the finger drains mode n at a rate proportional to X_n(s)^2, how much that mode moves under it. The modes that survive are the ones with a node right under the finger: \sin(n\pi s/L) = 0, which means ns/L is a whole number. At s = L/2 these are the even n, at 2f_1, 4f_1, 6f_1, \dots: a note with fundamental 2f_1. At s = L/3 they are n = 3, 6, 9, \dots, with fundamental 3f_1: an octave (a factor 2) and a fifth (a factor 3/2) up, since 2 \times 3/2 = 3.


The string’s motion is the sum of its modes, each swinging at its own frequency and fading at its own rate: 
u(x, t) = \sum_{n} a_n\,e^{-t/\tau_n}\sin\frac{n\pi x}{L}\,\cos(2\pi f_n t + \phi_n).
 The demo’s sound is made this way: it adds up these modes at f_n = n \times 196 Hz, each weighted by its push on the bridge, which is what reaches your ear (see “Where you pluck” below); the stems show how far each mode swings. Because every f_n is a whole multiple of f_1, apart from the slow fading the sum repeats every 1/f_1 seconds, and a sound that repeats is a note at that rate (page 0).
Where you pluck sets the brightness. A pluck starts each shape according to how much of it is in the plucked triangle. What reaches your ear is the string’s push on the bridge, and for the same height a shape with more arches has steeper ends, so it pushes harder. Pluck near the bridge, and the first several shapes push the bridge about equally hard (near the end, a shape with n arches starts about 1/n as large but is n times as steep, so the pushes come out about equal; fold below): the sound is bright. Pluck at the middle, and every shape with an even number of arches is missing, since those stand still exactly where you pulled; the rest push the bridge less and less, the more arches they have: a mellow, hollow sound.



Step-by-step derivationHow much of each shape a pluck starts uses integration by parts

Every shape of the string is a sum \sum_n b_n\sin(n\pi x/L) of its modes (second proof fold above), and b_n says how much of mode n the shape contains. A string pulled aside a distance d at a point x_p from one end, and let go, starts as a triangle. With x_p measured from the nut, where x = 0, its sine coefficients are 
b_n = \frac{2dL^2}{\pi^2 x_p(L - x_p)}\cdot\frac{\sin(n\pi x_p/L)}{n^2}.
 Measuring x_p from the bridge instead only flips the sign of every second b_n, since \sin(n\pi(L - x_p)/L) = \pm\sin(n\pi x_p/L), and signs do not change how loud a mode is; from here on x_p is the distance from the bridge. What reaches your ear is driven by the force on the bridge, which is proportional to the string’s slope there and so to n\,b_n for mode n. Near the bridge, x_p small, \sin(n\pi x_p/L) \approx n\pi x_p/L for the first several modes, so n b_n hardly falls off at all: the high modes are strong and the sound is bright. At the middle, \sin(n\pi/2) is zero for every even n, and the rest have n b_n falling like 1/n: a mellower, hollow sound.
Where the formula comes from. Take L = 1 and write q = x_p. The starting shape is u_0(x) = dx/q for 0 \le x \le q and u_0(x) = d(1 - x)/(1 - q) for q \le x \le 1. Its sine coefficients are b_n = 2\int_0^1 u_0(x)\sin(n\pi x)\,dx, by the perpendicularity of the sines, which the string inherits from the circle page. Integrate by parts twice on each straight piece. Since u_0 vanishes at both ends and u_0'' = 0 on each piece, the only term left comes from the jump in slope at the corner, from d/q just left of it to -d/(1-q) just right of it: b_n = \frac{2}{n^2\pi^2}\big(\tfrac{d}{q} + \tfrac{d}{1-q}\big)\sin(n\pi q) = \frac{2d\sin(n\pi q)}{n^2\pi^2 q(1-q)}. The 1/n^2 comes from that single corner.


Pressing down makes a new end. Pressing a finger firmly onto the fingerboard is different: it ties the string down there, and only the piece between the finger and the bridge sounds. By the formula for f_1, a shorter string sounds higher, in inverse proportion to its length: two-thirds of the length sounds a fifth up, half the length an octave up, and the semitone positions bunch closer together toward the bridge. Play a whole violin: press and hold a string to bow it, slide sideways to finger it, or switch to plucking.


  
  
    Bow (hold)Pizzicato, plucked (tap)
     Wooden body
    Press and hold a string. Slide left and right to finger it.
  
  
  Left edge: the nut; right edge: the bridge. Ticks: where the finger goes for each semitone (fold below). Stems: the partials you hear; switching the body off or on changes their heights, never their positions.





DetailsWhere the finger goes for each semitone uses powers

The nut is the end of the string near the tuning pegs, and an open string is one not pressed down by a finger. With the finger at distance s from the nut, the vibrating length shrinks to L - s, so the pitch rises by the factor L/(L - s). In equal temperament the twelve semitones of an octave are equal ratios of frequency, so each is 2^{1/12}, and k semitones are 2^{k/12}. Solving L/(L - s) = 2^{k/12} gives s_k = (1 - 2^{-k/12})L: the semitone positions bunch together toward the bridge. These are the ticks on the violin’s fingerboard above.


The bow locks the note. A bow grips the string, drags it along until the string’s pull tears it free, lets it slip back, and grips it again, once per period. By 1860 Hermann von Helmholtz had watched this through a vibration microscope: the string forms two straight pieces joined by one sharp corner, which races between the bridge and the finger. This is Helmholtz motion. It repeats exactly, so its partials sit exactly on the lines. (The demo’s bowed voice adds a gentle vibrato, as players do, which wobbles the lines slightly.) That matters because a real string is slightly stiff, and its own frequencies run a little sharp of the lines (page 7): plucked, each mode rings at its own slightly sharp frequency and fades; bowed, the stick and slip lock the whole motion into exact repetition. The locking comes from the bow’s friction, which is not linear; this page shows it but does not derive it.


    
    BowedPlucked at 1/4
    
    Slowed about 500 times. The faint lens-shaped outline is the path the corner traces. Stems: the partials of the push on the bridge.
  




Step-by-step derivationHelmholtz motion as a sum of modes uses the plucked-string formula above

A vibration microscope’s lens rides on a vibrating tuning fork, so that a bright speck on the string traces a pattern revealing its motion. Helmholtz reported what he saw in 1860 and in his 1863 book. The expansion of Helmholtz motion in the string’s eigenfunctions is, for some overall size a, 
u(x,t) = \sum_{n\ge1} \frac{a}{n^2}\,\sin\frac{n\pi x}{L}\,\sin(2\pi n f_1 t).
 Where this comes from: at each moment the string is two straight pieces, like a plucked string, with the corner at some point x_c. Helmholtz showed that the corner’s height is proportional to x_c(L - x_c), so it traces two arcs of a parabola, the lens in the demo, and that the corner moves at the wave speed c = 2Lf_1. Put that height in place of d in the pluck formula above: the factor x_c(L - x_c) cancels and b_n \propto \sin(n\pi x_c/L)/n^2. With x_c = 2Lf_1t this is \sin(2\pi nf_1t)/n^2; on the way back the corner runs along the lower arc, and the same formula covers it: for x_c between L and 2L, \sin(n\pi x_c/L) describes a corner at 2L - x_c with negative height. The motion repeats exactly every 1/f_1 seconds, so its partials sit exactly on nf_1. The force on the bridge is proportional to the string’s slope there, and the slope of \sin(n\pi x/L) carries an extra factor n\pi/L, so partial n pushes the bridge with strength proportional to 1/n. On an ideal string a pluck also gives exact multiples of f_1; the difference between plucking and bowing shows only on a real, slightly stiff string, as described above.


The body changes loudness, not pitch. The string itself moves very little air. It rocks the bridge, the bridge shakes the wooden body, and the body moves the air. Each step is linear: shaken at one frequency, it responds at that same frequency, only louder or quieter and a little delayed. So the body can change each partial’s height but can never move it to another frequency. Toggle the wooden body on the violin above: the stems change height and stay where they are.

title: Why does a light touch make a string jump an octave?
text:
What we found
Newton’s law on a short piece of string gave the wave equation, u_{tt} = c^2u_{xx}. Read as a rule, with the ends tied, it is the operator A = -c^2\,d^2/dx^2 on shapes that vanish at both ends. Its spectrum is \lambda_n = (n\pi c/L)^2, with eigenfunctions the arch shapes \sin(n\pi x/L), so the frequencies are exactly n f_1, with f_1 = \frac{1}{2L}\sqrt{T/\mu}: on the diagram, every stem on a line, and what we hear is a clear note. A light touch drains every mode that moves under the finger, so only the eigenfunctions already still there survive: at the middle, the even ones, a note an octave up. And the operator lesson: the rule for what the ends may do, a boundary condition, is part of the operator. It decides which shapes are allowed, and so which frequencies.

Same operator, different constants. Guitar, cello and harp strings obey the same equation with the same tied ends. They differ in length, tension and mass per length, which set the lowest frequency, and in how they are played: plucked (guitar, harp) or bowed (violin, cello).

title: What makes a sound a note?
text:
The pitch ruler
The stems under the wave are the note’s frequencies, drawn as multiples of 220 Hz: 1×, 2×, 3×, …. Those whole-number multiples are the lines of the pitch ruler, and every page of this series puts an instrument on it: stems on the pitch ruler, one per mode, make the spectrum diagram that stage 4 of every instrument page draws. A note’s frequencies sit on the lines. Take away the 1× stem and the rest still sit on lines of the same ruler, so the pitch is still 220 Hz. The component at the repetition rate itself is called the fundamental. Hearing the pitch without it is called the missing fundamental effect, and it is why a deep voice keeps its pitch over an ordinary telephone line, which cannot carry sounds below about 300 Hz.
Open “Mix your own” and try the presets. The stems’ heights change, and so does the sound’s color, its timbre, but the pitch stays put as long as the base frequency does. Keep only 2×, 4×, 6× and 8×, and the sound repeats twice as often: the base becomes 440 Hz, and the pitch jumps up an octave.

title: What makes a sound a note?
text:
How it works
A note is a pattern that repeats. Sound is air pressure rising and falling. When the pattern repeats, you hear a note, and its pitch is the repetition rate, measured in hertz. This holds for rates in the range where we hear pitch, from a few dozen to a few thousand times a second (for a recognizable melody, roughly 30 Hz to 4 or 5 kHz: Pressnitzer and colleagues measured the lower limit; the upper one is the traditional limit, which Oxenham and colleagues revisit). Much slower repetition is heard as a rhythm. Middle C, called C4, repeats about 262 times a second.
Every repeating sound is a chord on the lines. A pure tone is a single sine-shaped wave, the sound of a tuning fork. Any repeating pattern can be built from pure tones at 1, 2, 3, … times its repetition rate, and from no others; this is Fourier’s theorem, and page 3 shows where it comes from. These tones are the sound’s partials, and the one at the repetition rate itself is the fundamental. The repetition rate sets the pitch, whether or not the fundamental is actually there; the partials’ strengths set the timbre.
In symbols: sound is a pressure signal p(t). It is periodic with period P if p(t + P) = p(t) for every t; take P to be the shortest such time. The pitch is the repetition rate f = 1/P, for rates in the range where we hear pitch. Any periodic signal that is not too wild (continuous and made of smooth pieces is plenty) is the sum of its Fourier series: with f = 1/P, 
p(t) = \sum_{n \ge 0} b_n \cos(2\pi n f t + \phi_n) .
 The n = 0 term is a constant, the average pressure, usually zero. The possible frequencies nf are fixed by the period alone, and a given sound may use only some of them: a pure tone uses only f. The amplitudes b_n and the phases \phi_n carry everything else about the sound’s shape, and the ear is mostly insensitive to the phases.

A note, in symbols. A sound that repeats every P seconds contains only the frequencies f, 2f, 3f, \dots with f = 1/P: whole-number multiples of its repetition rate, which is its pitch.




Reader questionIs a musical note one frequency?

No. A note is a sound whose pressure repeats every P seconds, and its pitch is the repetition rate f = 1/P. By the Fourier series above, its components can only be at f, 2f, 3f, \dots, and usually several are present at once. The repetition rate sets the pitch, whether or not a component at f itself is present, and the weights b_n set the timbre: a piano C4 and a violin C4 share f and differ in their b_n. So a note corresponds to a period, not to a single frequency.


Why whole numbers matter. Turn it around. If something vibrates at several frequencies at once, its sound repeats only when they are all whole-number multiples of one common frequency. For two tones, the ratio of their frequencies must be a fraction, such as 3/2; the sound then repeats every 2 cycles of the lower tone. The reason is short. Write the ratio in lowest terms, f_2/f_1 = j/k, and wait P = k/f_1 seconds. In that time the lower tone completes f_1P = k whole cycles and the upper one f_2P = j whole cycles, so both are back where they started, and the sum begins again: it repeats every k cycles of the lower tone. A ratio like 1.59, which is 159/100, repeats only every 100 cycles of the lower tone, far too slowly to hear as one pitch. Try it:


  ▶ 2 : 1▶ 3 : 2▶ 1.59 : 1 (a drum)Play the slider's ratio
  Ratio2.00×
  
  
  Gray ticks mark cycles of the lower tone. At 2 : 1 the sum repeats every cycle; at 3 : 2 every two; at 1.59 : 1, which is 159/100, it lines up only after 100 cycles of the lower tone, far too slowly to hear as one pitch.


Not every instrument is exact. Frequencies very near whole-number multiples still sound like one note: a piano’s are slightly off, as page 7 shows, and it still plays notes. So the rule this series tests every instrument against reads: frequencies at, or very near, whole-number multiples of one frequency in the range we hear as pitch make a note.
Where the frequencies come from. This page took the frequencies as given. Every later page computes them. Newton’s law, applied to a small piece of the instrument, gives a rule that turns the instrument’s shape into the force pulling it back: the instrument’s operator. Writing the motion as u_{tt} = -A\,u, where u is the instrument’s shape (how far each point is from rest), u_{tt} its acceleration and A the operator, each special number \lambda of A, an eigenvalue, gives one frequency, f = \sqrt{\lambda}/2\pi. The list of eigenvalues is the operator’s spectrum. Whether the spectrum lands on the lines of the pitch ruler is the first test of whether the instrument plays a note; pages 6 and 6b show what the spectrum alone does not decide. The spectrum of an operator page sets out this recipe, from Newton’s law to what we hear, and runs it on every instrument.



ProofThe converse: if two tones repeat together, their ratio is a fraction, and the shortest period uses cosines and divisibility

Let s(t) = \cos(2\pi f_1 t) + \cos(2\pi f_2 t) with 0 < f_1 < f_2.
If the ratio is rational, s is periodic. Write f_2/f_1 = j/k in lowest terms and put P = k/f_1. Then f_1P = k and f_2P = j are whole numbers, so both cosines return to their starting values after time P, and s(t+P) = s(t).
If s is periodic, the ratio is rational. Suppose s(t+P) = s(t) for all t, with P > 0. At t = 0 this gives s(P) = s(0) = 2. A sum of two cosines equals 2 only when both cosines equal 1, so \cos(2\pi f_1P) = \cos(2\pi f_2P) = 1, which means f_1P and f_2P are whole numbers. So f_2/f_1 = (f_2P)/(f_1P) is a ratio of whole numbers. Since f_2/f_1 = j/k, we have k\,(f_2P) = j\,(f_1P), so k divides j\,(f_1P); as j and k share no factor, k divides the whole number f_1P. So every period is a multiple of k/f_1, and k/f_1 is the shortest one.
The shortest period k/f_1 grows with the denominator k. A ratio like 1.59 = 159/100 is rational, but its pattern repeats only every 100 cycles of the lower tone, far too slowly for the ear to hear as one pitch. How the ear decides what counts as “simple enough”, and how near to whole-number multiples is near enough, are questions of perception, not mathematics; see pitch.

title: What makes a sound a note?
text:
What we found
A note is a sound that repeats, and its pitch is how often it repeats. So a note’s frequencies sit on the lines of one pitch ruler, whole-number multiples of one base frequency, and that base frequency need not be present itself. Every later page derives an instrument’s operator from Newton’s law, computes its spectrum, and puts the frequencies on this ruler: on the lines, a note; off the lines, a clang or a thud.

Listen first: tap a tine. Then tick the box that keeps the overtones ringing, and tap it again.

title: Why does a kalimba sound clean?
section: 1 · Newton’s law: the equation of motion
text:
1 · Newton’s law: the equation of motion
Mathematics used: partial derivatives, an integral over a cross-section, cosh and sinh, and a 2×2 determinant (all explained).
A string is held straight by tension. A tine is under no tension at all: it springs back because steel resists being bent. To find the force behind that, we apply Newton’s law, mass times acceleration equals force, to one thin slice of the tine.
Let u(x, t) be the tine’s height at distance x from the clamp at time t; subscripts are partial derivatives, so u_{xx} is the curvature, how sharply the tine bends. The tine is steel of Young’s modulus E (how stiff the steel is) and density \rho, with cross-section area S.
1. Bending stretches the outside and squeezes the inside. Bend the bar. Fibers on the outside of the curve stretch and fibers on the inside compress, while a middle line, the neutral axis, keeps its length.

  
  
  
  
  stretched (y > 0)compressed (y < 0)
  neutral axis, y = 0

For a gentle bend, a fiber at height y above the neutral axis is stretched by the fraction -y\,u_{xx}: its distance from the axis times how fast the bar turns per unit length. (The minus sign: where u_{xx} < 0 the bar bends down, and its top side, y > 0, is on the outside of the curve and stretched.) By Hooke’s law the fiber then carries the stress (force per area) -E\,y\,u_{xx}. Summed over the cross-section, these forces cancel, which is what places the neutral axis through the middle (the centroid) of the cross-section; but their turning effects do not cancel. Add them up over the small bits of area dA of the cross-section S, each pulling with stress times dA at lever arm y; the total is the bending moment 
\begin{aligned}
M &= -\int_S y\,(-E\,y\,u_{xx})\,dA = E\,u_{xx}\int_S y^2\,dA \\
&= EI\,u_{xx} .
\end{aligned}
 The number I = \int_S y^2\,dA, the second moment of area, says how the cross-section’s shape resists bending. For a rectangle of width w and thickness h, the strip at height y has area w\,dy, so I = \int_{-h/2}^{h/2} y^2\,w\,dy = wh^3/12; for a round wire of diameter d, I = \pi d^4/64.
2. A change in bending moment along the tine is a sideways force. A moment turns a slice but cannot lift it. Each face of a slice also carries a vertical force, the shear force V. The conventions: M is the moment on a face that bends the slice into an upward curve, counterclockwise on the right face and clockwise on the left; V is the upward force on the right face, and the left face feels the same force downward.

  
  
  
  
  
  
  MM + dM
  VV + dVdx

We neglect the slice’s resistance to being spun, its rotational inertia, which is accurate when the bar is thin compared with the length of its bending waves; then the turning effects on the slice must balance. Taking them about the left face, the shear on the right face times the lever arm dx cancels the change in moment: V\,dx + dM = 0, so 
V = -M_x = -EI\,u_{xxx} .

3. Newton’s law on the slice. The vertical forces on the two faces do not balance: their difference, V(x + dx) - V(x) = V_x\,dx, accelerates the slice’s mass \rho S\,dx. So 
\rho S\,u_{tt} = V_x = -EI\,u_{xxxx} .
 Dividing by the mass per length \rho S, this is the Euler–Bernoulli beam equation, u_{tt} = -\kappa^2 u_{xxxx} with \kappa^2 = EI/\rho S.
What we assumed. Small slopes; a uniform bar; no rotational inertia of the slices (Rayleigh’s correction for it adds a small term that matters only for thick bars and high modes); no shear deformation of the slices (Timoshenko’s correction); a tine clamped at exactly one point; and no damping or sound radiation: in this model every mode rings forever, and how fast the overtone dies is taken from measurement (stage 5).

title: Why does a kalimba sound clean?
text:
2 · The operator
Read the beam equation as a rule: take the tine’s shape, differentiate it four times along the tine, and multiply by \kappa^2. That is minus the restoring force per unit mass, the tine’s operator A = \kappa^2\,d^4/dx^4, and the equation reads u_{tt} = -Au.
The ends. At the base the tine is held down, so it can neither move nor tilt: u = 0 and u_x = 0. A bar held this way at one end and free at the other is called a cantilever. At the free tip nothing pushes or bends the bar, so both the moment and the shear force vanish: u_{xx} = 0 and u_{xxx} = 0. That is two conditions at each end, four in all, as a fourth-order operator needs; they are part of the operator, as the tied ends were for the string.

The tine’s operator. 
\begin{gathered}
u_{tt} = -A\,u, \qquad A = \kappa^2\,\frac{d^4}{dx^4}, \\
\kappa^2 = \frac{EI}{\rho S},
\end{gathered}
 with u = u_x = 0 at the clamp and u_{xx} = u_{xxx} = 0 at the tip. In words: the force per unit mass pulling each point back is the fourth derivative of the shape, times a constant set by the steel and the cross-section. The string’s operator was -c^2\,d^2/dx^2: two derivatives instead of four.

What four derivatives do. Squeeze a shape into half the length, and every rate of change along it doubles. A string’s pull depends on its curvature, how sharply it bends, a rate of change of a rate of change: 2 × 2 = 4 times harder. A tine’s push depends on how that curvature itself changes along the tine, twice over: 2 × 2 × 2 × 2 = 16 times harder. Both of the tine’s surprises in stage 5 come from this.

title: Why does a kalimba sound clean?
text:
3 · Its spectrum
A mode is a shape X(x) that the operator only rescales, A X = \lambda X. Such a shape swings as X(x)\cos\omega t with \omega = \sqrt\lambda, at the frequency f = \sqrt\lambda/2\pi. The list of all the eigenvalues \lambda is the operator’s spectrum. For the tine, the mode equation is 
\kappa^2 X'''' = \lambda X .

1. Which shapes does the operator only rescale? Write \lambda = \kappa^2\beta^4, so that X'''' = \beta^4 X: four derivatives give back the shape, times \beta^4. The number \beta plays the role of the string’s wavenumber. Four functions do this: \cos\beta x, \sin\beta x, \cosh\beta x and \sinh\beta x, where \cosh y = (e^y + e^{-y})/2 and \sinh y = (e^y - e^{-y})/2 are the hyperbolic functions. Differentiating the definitions, (\cosh y)' = \sinh y and (\sinh y)' = \cosh y, with no sign changes, so the hyperbolic pair gives back \beta^4 times itself after four derivatives, just as \cos and \sin do after their sign flips cancel; multiplying out the definitions also gives \cosh^2 y - \sinh^2 y = 1, and \cosh 0 = 1, \sinh 0 = 0. So X is a combination of the four, with four unknown constants, and the four end conditions are four equations for them.
2. Hold the clamped end still. X(0) = 0 and X'(0) = 0 leave two constants: 
\begin{aligned}
X = {}&a\,(\cos\beta x - \cosh\beta x) \\
&+ b\,(\sin\beta x - \sinh\beta x) .
\end{aligned}

3. Leave the free tip unbent and unpushed. Differentiating, and dropping the common factors \beta^2 and \beta^3, the conditions X''(L) = 0 and X'''(L) = 0 read, with the shorthand c_1 = \cos\beta L, s_1 = \sin\beta L, c_2 = \cosh\beta L, s_2 = \sinh\beta L: 
\begin{gathered}
-(c_1 + c_2)\,a - (s_1 + s_2)\,b = 0, \\
(s_1 - s_2)\,a - (c_1 + c_2)\,b = 0 .
\end{gathered}

4. When is there a mode? Two equations pa + qb = 0 and ra + sb = 0 have a solution other than a = b = 0 exactly when ps - qr = 0, the determinant (solve the first for a and substitute into the second). Here 
\begin{aligned}
&(c_1 + c_2)^2 + (s_1 + s_2)(s_1 - s_2) \\
&\quad = c_1^2 + s_1^2 + 2c_1c_2 + c_2^2 - s_2^2 \\
&\quad = 2 + 2c_1c_2 = 0,
\end{aligned}
 using c_1^2 + s_1^2 = 1 and c_2^2 - s_2^2 = 1. So the tine has a mode exactly when 
\cos\beta L\,\cosh\beta L = -1 .

5. Find the roots. Since \cosh\beta L grows fast, \cos\beta L must be close to 0, so \beta L sits near (n - \tfrac12)\pi, closer and closer as n grows. Solved numerically, the roots are \beta L = 1.8751,\ 4.6941,\ 7.8548,\ 10.9955, \dots; the first is the furthest from its estimate, \pi/2 \approx 1.571, because the clamp and the free tip shift it most.

The tine’s spectrum. The modes are X_n = \cosh\beta_n x - \cos\beta_n x - \sigma_n(\sinh\beta_n x - \sin\beta_n x), which is step 2 with a = -1 and b = \sigma_n = (\sinh\beta_nL - \sin\beta_nL)/(\cosh\beta_nL + \cos\beta_nL), from the second equation of step 3 (the first gives (c_1 + c_2)/(s_1 + s_2), the same number at every root, by the mode condition). Their eigenvalues are \lambda_n = \kappa^2\beta_n^4, and their frequencies are 
f_n = \frac{\sqrt{\lambda_n}}{2\pi} = \frac{\kappa\,\beta_n^2}{2\pi} = \frac{\kappa\,(\beta_nL)^2}{2\pi L^2} .
 Since f_n \propto (\beta_nL)^2, the frequency ratios are 1 : 6.27 : 17.55 : 34.39 : \cdots, growing like {(2n-1)^2}: off the whole numbers.

Compare pinned ends. A bar held in place at both ends but free to pivot has u = u_{xx} = 0 at each end. Then the shapes \sin(n\pi x/L) satisfy all four conditions, four derivatives multiply them by (n\pi/L)^4, and the ratios are 1 : 4 : 9 : 16: whole numbers. If every root of the clamped–free tine sat exactly at (n - \tfrac12)\pi, its ratios would be the whole numbers 1 : 9 : 25 too; the shift of the first root is what puts them off the lines.



ProofWhy the eigenvalues are real and positive, and the modes perpendicular uses integration by parts

The operator d^4/dx^4 with these four conditions is symmetric, by integrating by parts four times (the boundary terms all vanish), so its eigenvalues are real and its eigenfunctions perpendicular, as on the circle; with the right domain it is also self-adjoint. Integrating by parts twice gives \int_0^L X\,X''''\,dx = \int_0^L (X'')^2\,dx, so no eigenvalue is negative, and zero is ruled out because X'' = 0 with a clamped base forces X = 0. That is why \beta is a real, positive number.

title: Why does a kalimba sound clean?
text:
4 · On the spectrum diagram
Here are one tine’s frequencies from the result box, as multiples of the lowest: 1×, then 6.27×, far from the gray whole-number lines, and further up 17.55× and 34.39×, off the right edge. Each stem’s height is how hard that mode pushes sideways on the bridge just after a pluck, one of the two loads a tine puts on the bridge (the fold in stage 5 has both). Tap a stem to see the shape of that mode.

title: Why does a kalimba sound clean?
text:
5 · What we hear
Why the note still sounds clean. You might guess the overtone is too quiet to hear. It isn’t. In how far the tine swings, the overtone is tiny; but the body hears the push on the bridge, not the swing, and in that push the overtone starts strong (fold below). That strong start is the click at the beginning of each note. What keeps the note clean is that the overtone dies within a fraction of a second, while the fundamental rings on, and the fundamental left on its own is a clean note. Why it dies so fast is not computed here; the page takes it from measurement. The acoustician D. M. F. Chapman found exactly this pattern on a real kalimba: one dominant overtone, at 5.9 to 6.8 times the fundamental, gone soon after the attack. With the box ticked, the off-line overtones keep ringing, and the same tine clangs like a bell.



Step-by-step derivationHow strongly a pluck at the tip excites each mode uses integration by parts

Chapman measured the tines of one kalimba, a Hugh Tracey pentatonic, and found one dominant overtone at 5.9 to 6.8 times the fundamental, near the ideal 6.27, dying away quickly after the attack. A real tine is clamped a little behind the bridge and rests on the bridge partway along, rather than being perfectly clamped at one point, and he found that the measured ratios depend on how the bridge divides the tine’s length, which is one reason they spread. The steps below compute, for the ideal tine, how much of each mode a pluck starts. In short: in displacement, the second mode starts at only 2.5% of the first; but at the clamp, where in this ideal model the tine presses on the bridge, it starts at about 16% of the first in bending moment and 55% in shear force. Those are two different measures of the push on the bridge, not a range of uncertainty.

The pluck shape. Before release, a push F at the tip holds the tine still in a bent shape u_0, so the bar’s restoring force balances the push.
Split it into modes. Write u_0 = \sum_n a_n X_n, with each mode scaled so that \int_0^L X_n^2\,dx = L. Inside the tine nothing pushes, so EI\,u_0'''' = 0 there; the push enters only at the tip, as the shear force there. Now compute \int_0^L EI\,u_0\,X_n''''\,dx in two ways. First, EI\,X_n'''' = \rho S\,\omega_n^2X_n (the mode equation), and the modes are perpendicular, so only the a_n term survives: the integral is \rho S L\,\omega_n^2\,a_n. Second, integrate by parts four times to move the derivatives onto u_0, as in the proof fold above. Inside, EI\,u_0'''' = 0; at the clamp both u_0 and X_n vanish with their slopes; at the tip X_n'' = X_n''' = 0 and u_0'' = 0. The one term left is the tip’s shear force times X_n(L), which is F\,X_n(L). So \rho S L\,\omega_n^2\,a_n = F\,X_n(L). This is page 1’s spring again: mode n is a spring of stiffness proportional to \omega_n^2, pushed with a force proportional to its value at the tip, and it gives way by force over stiffness.
Tip values. Use the modes in the standard form of the spectrum box above, with \sigma_n about 0.734 and 1.018 for the first two modes. Written this way, each mode already has \int_0^L X_n^2\,dx = L, and its tip value is \pm2 for every n (a known property of clamped–free modes, easily confirmed numerically). So a_n \propto 1/\omega_n^2, and a_2/a_1 = 1/6.27^2 \approx 2.5\%.
Forces. In this model the tine is clamped right at the bridge, so the forces at the clamp are the forces on the bridge. The bending moment at the clamp is EI\,u_{xx} there, and the shear force EI\,u_{xxx} there (up to sign). From the standard form, X_n''(0) = 2\beta_n^2 and X_n'''(0) = -2\sigma_n\beta_n^3. Multiplying by a_n \propto 1/\omega_n^2 \propto 1/\beta_n^4, the second mode’s moment at the clamp is (\beta_1/\beta_2)^2 = (1.875/4.694)^2 \approx 16\% of the first’s, and its shear force (\sigma_2/\sigma_1)(\beta_1/\beta_2) \approx 1.39 \times 0.40 \approx 55\%.



A plucked tine moves as the sum of its modes, u = \sum_n a_n X_n(x)\cos(2\pi f_n t + \phi_n), each mode fading at its own rate. The demo’s sound is made exactly this way: it adds up the first five modes at the frequencies of stage 3, each starting with its shear-force strength from the fold above (55% for the second mode), as in stage 4. The fundamental fades over a couple of seconds and the overtones within a small fraction of that; those fading rates are an illustrative choice consistent with Chapman’s observation, not computed. Tick the box and every mode fades as slowly as the fundamental.
Overtones off the lines. Higher modes bend in shorter humps, and for a tine shorter humps push back much harder, so the frequencies grow like the square of the mode number instead of the number itself. Where exactly they land is set by the four end conditions: pinned ends would give the whole numbers 1, 4, 9, 16, but a tine is clamped at one end and free at the other, and its spectrum is 1, 6.27, 17.55, …, off the lines.
Half the length, two octaves up. The result box says f_n = \kappa(\beta_nL)^2/(2\pi L^2), and the numbers \beta_nL do not depend on the length: so a tine’s frequency goes as one over its length squared. Half the length gives 4 times the frequency, two octaves, where a string, with f \propto 1/L, rises only an octave. That is why the low tines in the demo are not twice as long as the high ones an octave up. Kalimba makers tune a tine by sliding it over the bridge to change its free length (Kalimba Magic), and the 1/L^2 makes a small slide go a long way.

title: Why does a kalimba sound clean?
text:
What we found
Newton’s law on a thin slice of bent steel gave the beam equation, u_{tt} = -\kappa^2 u_{xxxx}. Read as a rule, with the tine clamped at one end and free at the other, it is the operator A = \kappa^2\,d^4/dx^4. Its spectrum, from \cos\beta L\cosh\beta L = -1, puts the frequencies at 1 : 6.27 : 17.55 : 34.39, growing like the square of the mode number: on the diagram, the overtones sit far off the whole-number lines, and by the series’ rule the tine should clang. What we hear is clean, because the off-line overtones die almost at once and leave the fundamental ringing alone. The operator taught two things on the way: four derivatives make the frequencies spread apart like the squares, and the way the ends are held decides whether they land on whole numbers.

Same math elsewhere. Harmonica reeds and the steel comb of a music box are also bars held at one end and free at the other.
