title: Where did the harmonica reed’s overtones go?
text:
← 6 Kalimba · The Shape of a Sound · Spectrum of an operator · Map · 7 Piano →
Listen first: pluck the reed, then blow it, and compare the stems with the gray whole-number lines.

title: Where did the harmonica reed’s overtones go?
section: 1 · Newton’s law: the equation of motion
text:
1 · Newton’s law: the equation of motion
Mathematics used: partial derivatives, as on page 6, plus Fourier series (page 3).
A reed is a thin brass bar, riveted at one end over a slot and free at the other: the same kind of bar as a kalimba tine. So Newton’s law on one thin slice of it goes exactly as on the kalimba page, which derives each step with figures. In short, with u(x, t) the reed’s sideways displacement at distance x from the rivet, \rho the density of brass and S the area of the reed’s cross-section:
1. Bending stretches the outside and squeezes the inside. The turning effects of those stretched and squeezed fibers add up to the bending moment M = EI\,u_{xx}, where E is brass’s Young’s modulus and I the second moment of area of the cross-section.
2. A change in bending along the reed means a sideways force. The turning effects on a thin slice balance, so the sideways force across each cut is V = -M_x = -EI\,u_{xxx}.
3. Newton’s law on the slice. The difference of the sideways forces on the slice’s two faces accelerates its mass \rho S\,dx: 
\rho S\,u_{tt} = V_x = -EI\,u_{xxxx} .

What we assumed. As on the kalimba page: small motions, a uniform bar clamped at exactly one point, no rotational inertia or shear deformation of the slices. Also no damping and no air around the reed: in the model every mode rings forever. Real reeds are not exactly uniform, so their overtones differ somewhat from the ideal values below.

title: Where did the harmonica reed’s overtones go?
text:
2 · The operator
Dividing by the mass per unit length \rho S puts the equation in the series’ form u_{tt} = -A\,u. The ends complete the operator: at the rivet the reed can neither move nor tilt, u = u_x = 0; at the free tip nothing bends or pushes it, u_{xx} = u_{xxx} = 0.

The reed’s operator is the tine’s: 
\begin{gathered}
u_{tt} = -A\,u, \qquad A = \kappa^2\,\frac{d^4}{dx^4}, \\
\kappa^2 = \frac{EI}{\rho S} = \frac{E h^2}{12\rho},
\end{gathered}
 with u = u_x = 0 at the rivet and u_{xx} = u_{xxx} = 0 at the tip. The last form of \kappa^2 is for a rectangular reed of width w and thickness h, where I = wh^3/12 and S = wh. In words: the force per unit mass pulling each point back is the fourth derivative of the shape, times a constant set by the brass and the thickness.

title: Where did the harmonica reed’s overtones go?
text:
3 · Its spectrum
A mode is a shape the operator only rescales, AX = \lambda X; it swings at the angular frequency \sqrt\lambda, so its frequency is f = \sqrt\lambda/2\pi, and the list of eigenvalues is the spectrum. The operator and the end conditions are the tine’s, so the spectrum is too. The kalimba page writes \lambda = \kappa^2\beta^4, solves the four end conditions, and finds a mode exactly when \cos\beta L\,\cosh\beta L = -1, with roots \beta L = 1.8751,\ 4.6941,\ 7.8548, \dots; the angular frequencies are \sqrt\lambda = \kappa\beta^2.

The reed’s spectrum. Eigenvalues \lambda_n = \kappa^2\beta_n^4, frequencies f_n = \kappa\beta_n^2/2\pi, in the ratios 1 : 6.27 : 17.55 : \cdots, off the whole-number lines, with the lowest 
f_1 = \frac{(1.8751)^2}{2\pi}\cdot\frac{h}{L^2}\sqrt{\frac{E}{12\rho}} .
 The width w cancels: it decides how much air the reed moves, not its pitch. Low reeds are long, high reeds are short.

title: Where did the harmonica reed’s overtones go?
text:
4 · On the spectrum diagram
Plucked, the stems (below, and in the demo at the top) are the spectrum just computed: 1\times, then the overtones at 6.27\times and 17.55\times, off the gray lines, dying almost at once, as on the kalimba. Blown, the stems sit at 1\times, 2\times, 3\times, 4\times, \dots, every one on a line, and none at 6.27\times. Each stem’s height is how strong that frequency is in the sound. Same reed, same operator; only the way it is played differs. Stage 5 explains the blown stems.


  
  
  Plucked (top): 1× and 6.27×, off the lines (17.55× is off the right edge). Blown (bottom): every stem on a line, none at 6.27×.

title: Where did the harmonica reed’s overtones go?
text:
5 · What we hear
Blown, the reed’s own overtones never reach the sound. Blowing turns the reed into a valve that chops the air into puffs, and the puffs repeat exactly; a sound that repeats has frequencies only at whole-number multiples of its rate, so 6.27× and 17.55× have nowhere to appear. The steps below show why; first, what a pluck gives.
Plucked: you hear the spectrum. A plucked reed rings at its own frequencies, the result box of stage 3: the reed moves as \sum_n a_n X_n \cos(2\pi f_n t + \phi_n), so the sound is a sum of tones at the frequencies f_n, each fading at its own rate (damping, added to the model). The overtones at 6.27 and 17.55 times the fundamental are off the lines and die fast, just like a kalimba tine’s. The demo’s plucked sound is synthesized exactly this way.
Blown: the reed becomes a valve. Blow, and the reed swings through its slot, opening and closing the air path hundreds of times a second. The sound comes mainly from the chopped airflow; the acoustics writer Colin Pykett notes that very little comes from the reed’s own motion. A steadily blown reed settles into a motion that repeats itself exactly, at a playing frequency f_p slightly below its first mode’s, so the puffs of air repeat at that rate too. Why the reed locks into one repeating motion is observed, and reproduced by computer models of reeds, but not derived here (fold below). Granting that it does, the rest is mathematics:

The airflow repeats. Let q(t) be the airflow through the slot. In the steady oscillation it repeats every P = 1/f_p seconds: q(t + P) = q(t).
A repeating function is a Fourier series. By the circle page, a function of period P is a sum of \cos(2\pi nt/P) and \sin(2\pi nt/P) for n = 0, 1, 2, \dots, so it contains only the frequencies n f_p.
So the note lands on the lines. The blown sound has frequencies only at whole-number multiples of the playing frequency, with strong odd and even multiples (Pykett). How strong each one is depends on the shape of a single puff: short, sharp puffs give strong high partials.

The argument uses only that the motion repeats, not which modes make it up. That is why the reed’s own overtone frequencies, 6.27 and 17.55 times f_1, do not appear in a steadily blown note: that is where they went.



DetailsWhy the reed locks into one repeating motion, and how the demo makes its sound

A steady oscillation kept going by a steady push, like this one, is called a self-sustained oscillation, and the repeating cycle it settles into a limit cycle; the bowed string and the clarinet reed are others. That the blown reed settles into one is observed, and reproduced by nonlinear models of reeds; it is not derived here. A plausible picture, not a derivation: the airflow feeds energy mainly into the first mode, the other modes are not kept going at their own frequencies, and in the repeating cycle they move only as they are pushed, at whole-number multiples of f_p.
The demos’ blown sounds are models. The “Blow the C5 reed” and filing demos play one puff shape, chosen so that the open part of each cycle is short, repeated at the playing frequency: its whole-number multiples weaker overall as they go up. The chromatic harmonica further down passes the same puff train through two broad peaks, a stand-in for resonances of the player’s mouth and the instrument, and adds a little band-passed breath noise. The peaks were set by ear, not measured, so the timbre is approximate. The pitch and the whole-number spacing are not approximations.


The same mechanism drives the bowed string and the clarinet: a steady push, from the bow or the breath, turned into a sound that repeats. On those instruments the string’s or tube’s own frequencies already sit nearly on the lines, so the push and the instrument agree, and locking is easy. A free reed’s own overtones are far off the lines, which lets you hear that the way it is driven, not the reed’s own frequencies, decides where a blown note’s overtones sit.
Tuning a reed with a file. Reed makers tune by scraping metal off, and where they scrape decides the direction. The first mode bends most near the rivet and moves most near the tip. Thin the reed near the rivet and you remove stiffness where it counts: the pitch drops. Thin it near the tip and you remove mass where it counts: the pitch rises. It is the spring of page 1 again, where frequency grows with stiffness and falls with mass. Try it below.


    Where to filebase
    
    Blow the filed reedBlow the original
    Filing removes a quarter of the thickness over about a tenth of the reed. The pitch change is estimated as in the fold below.
  




Step-by-step derivationWhy filing moves the pitch: stiffness against mass uses integration by parts and a first-order approximation

The Rayleigh quotient explains the direction. For the first mode, 
\omega_1^2 = \min_{u} \frac{\int_0^L EI\,(u'')^2\,dx}{\int_0^L \rho S\,u^2\,dx},
 the minimum taken over shapes, not identically zero, that satisfy the conditions at the rivet; the minimizing shape is the first mode itself. This is \omega^2 = k/m from page 1 again: stiffness on top, weighted by where the reed bends, and mass at the bottom, weighted by where it moves. The first mode bends most near the rivet and moves most near the tip. Thinning the reed near the rivet removes stiffness where it counts and lowers the pitch; thinning it near the tip removes mass where it counts and raises it. The steps below make this quantitative.

The quotient. Multiply \rho S\,\omega^2X = (EI\,X'')'' by X and integrate by parts twice; the boundary terms vanish at the rivet and at the free tip, as on the kalimba page. This gives \omega^2 = \int EI(X'')^2 / \int \rho S X^2 for every mode.
Small change. File the reed so that its thickness changes by \delta h(x) < 0. Then I \propto h^3 changes by \delta(EI) = 3EI\,\delta h/h, and S \propto h changes by \delta(\rho S) = \rho S\,\delta h/h, to first order, that is, ignoring terms in (\delta h)^2.
First order. Because the first mode minimizes the quotient, changing the shape slightly changes the quotient only by an amount proportional to the square of the change. So to first order one may keep the old mode shape X and change only the coefficients: 
\delta(\omega^2) = \frac{\int \frac{\delta h}{h}\,\big(3EI\,(X'')^2 - \omega^2\rho S\,X^2\big)\,dx}{\int \rho S\,X^2\,dx}.

Sign. Near the rivet X \approx 0 and X'' is largest, so the bracket is positive and, with \delta h < 0, \omega drops. Near the tip X'' = 0 and X is largest, so the bracket is negative and \omega rises. In between there is a point where filing changes nothing, to first order.

The demo uses the full quotient with the original mode shape, which is accurate to first order in the depth of filing.


The chromatic slide. A chromatic harmonica has two sets of reed chambers, the second tuned a semitone higher. Each hole has a blow reed, sounded by breathing out, and a draw reed, sounded by breathing in, in each set. Pushing the slide moves a perforated bar that closes one set and opens the other, so every note rises a semitone. In solo tuning, the usual layout for a chromatic harmonica, each group of four holes holds C, E, G, C on the blow and D, F, A, B on the draw. Here is a whole one to play.


  blow, breathing out (top row: keys 1 … =)draw, breathing in (bottom row: keys Q … ])
  
  
    Slide (hold, or Space)
    Press and hold a hole. Slide across holes to move between notes.
  
  Twelve holes in solo tuning (explained just above), from C4, middle C, up three octaves. Pushing the slide raises every note a semitone, by switching the air to a second set of reeds.

title: Where did the harmonica reed’s overtones go?
text:
What we found
Newton’s law on a slice of brass (stage 1) gave the reed the kalimba tine’s operator (stage 2), \kappa^2\,d^4/dx^4, riveted at one end and free at the other, and the same spectrum (stage 3), 1 : 6.27 : 17.55, off the whole-number lines (stage 4). Plucked, that spectrum is what you hear, and the overtones die fast. Blown, the reed chops the air into puffs that repeat, and a repeating sound has frequencies only on the lines, so you hear a clean note. The operator decides the frequencies an object vibrates at on its own; a steady drive can lock it into others, and decides what you hear.

Same operator as the kalimba. Accordion, concertina and harmonium reeds are free reeds too: they swing freely through a slot, unlike a clarinet’s reed, which beats against the mouthpiece. All of them are cantilevers like the kalimba’s tine: same operator, same ends, smaller and thinner, usually of brass in harmonicas and harmoniums and of steel in accordions and concertinas. What separates a harmonica from a kalimba is the excitation, steady airflow instead of one pluck.

title: Why does a fading note stay in tune?
text:
← 0 Note · The Shape of a Sound · Spectrum of an operator · Map · 2 Beads →
Listen first: change how far you pull the mass, and watch how long each bob takes.

title: Why does a fading note stay in tune?
section: 1 · Newton’s law: the equation of motion
text:
1 · Newton’s law: the equation of motion
Mathematics used: second derivatives.
Every page of this series runs the same recipe: apply Newton’s law, mass times acceleration equals force, to one piece of the instrument; find that the force is a fixed rule applied to the instrument’s shape; read off that rule, the operator; find its spectrum; and from the spectrum, what we hear. The spectrum of an operator page sets out the recipe in general. For one mass on a spring, the “shape” is a single number, how far the mass is from rest.
1. The spring pulls back in proportion to the stretch. Twice as far, twice the pull: this is Hooke’s law. With x the distance from the resting position (for a hanging spring, the position where the spring’s pull balances gravity) and k the spring’s stiffness, the force is 
F = -k\,x ,
 where the minus sign says the pull points back toward rest.
2. The pull sets the acceleration. Force equals mass times acceleration. Writing \ddot x for the acceleration, the second derivative of x with respect to time, 
m\,\ddot x = -k\,x .

What we assumed. The pull is exactly proportional to the stretch (Hooke’s law holds), the spring itself has no mass, and nothing else acts on the mass: no friction for now.

title: Why does a fading note stay in tune?
text:
2 · The operator
Divide by the mass. The acceleration is the displacement multiplied by one fixed number, k/m, with its direction reversed: 
\ddot x = -\frac{k}{m}\,x .


The operator. \ddot x = -A\,x, where A is the rule “multiply by k/m”. For any displacement x, A\,x is the restoring force per unit mass with its direction reversed; the minus sign stays in the equation, as on every later page. There is nothing to hold at the ends here: a single mass has no boundary. In words: this is the smallest possible operator, acting on a single number.

title: Why does a fading note stay in tune?
text:
3 · Its spectrum
A mode is a motion in which the shape keeps its form and only its size swings, at one frequency. In operator language, a mode’s shape X is one the operator only rescales, A X = \lambda X; the rescaling factor \lambda is an eigenvalue, and the list of all eigenvalues is the operator’s spectrum. Here every displacement is simply multiplied by k/m, so the spectrum is one number, \lambda = k/m. Now find the motion it allows.
1. Try a steady swing. Guess x = a\cos(\omega t + \phi), with amplitude a, starting phase \phi and angular frequency \omega in radians per second.
2. Differentiate twice and see what comes back. \cos \to -\omega\sin \to -\omega^2\cos: two derivatives give -\omega^2 times the start, 
\ddot x = -\omega^2\,a\cos(\omega t + \phi) = -\omega^2\,x .

3. Match the equation. This equals -\lambda x exactly when \omega^2 = \lambda. The cosine repeats each time \omega t grows by 2\pi, so the motion repeats f = \omega/2\pi times a second: 
f = \frac{\sqrt{\lambda}}{2\pi} = \frac{1}{2\pi}\sqrt{\frac{k}{m}} .
 The amplitude a and the phase \phi are free: they record how you started the motion, and they do not appear in f.

The spectrum. One eigenvalue, \lambda = k/m. One angular frequency, \omega = \sqrt{\lambda}, and one frequency, f = \frac{1}{2\pi}\sqrt{k/m}, whatever the amplitude. In words: the same recipe, frequency = square root of an eigenvalue, divided by 2\pi, gives every frequency in the rest of the series.




ProofEvery motion is of this form, and the pitch cannot depend on amplitude uses the uniqueness of solutions of a differential equation

Every solution is a\cos(\omega t + \phi). The equation \ddot x = -\lambda x is linear: sums and multiples of solutions are solutions. A solution is determined by its starting position x(0) and starting velocity \dot x(0); this is the uniqueness theorem for ordinary differential equations. The functions \cos\omega t and \sin\omega t, with \omega = \sqrt\lambda, are solutions with starting data (1, 0) and (0, \omega). So the solution with data (x_0, v_0) is x_0\cos\omega t + (v_0/\omega)\sin\omega t. By the formula \cos(\omega t + \phi) = \cos\omega t\cos\phi - \sin\omega t\sin\phi, this equals a\cos(\omega t + \phi) with a = \sqrt{x_0^2 + (v_0/\omega)^2}, \cos\phi = x_0/a and \sin\phi = -v_0/(\omega a).
Amplitude cannot change the pitch. If x(t) is a solution, so is 2x(t), by linearity, and it has the same period.

title: Why does a fading note stay in tune?
text:
4 · On the spectrum diagram
One eigenvalue means one stem on the pitch ruler: a pure tone, at f = \sqrt{k/m}/2\pi. The readout in the demo above is exactly this formula. The frequency goes as the square root of stiffness over mass: four times the stiffness doubles it, four times the mass halves it, and the size of the pull never enters. A note needs more than one stem; the next page finds where the others come from.

title: Why does a fading note stay in tune?
text:
5 · What we hear
Twice the swing, the same time. The frequency formula contains k and m but not the amplitude. In plain words: take any motion of the mass and double it, twice as far from rest at every moment. The pull doubles too, so the acceleration doubles, which is exactly what the doubled motion needs. So the doubled motion is also a motion of the mass, and it repeats just as often. That is why a fading note keeps its pitch.
The motion is the one mode, x = a\cos(2\pi f t + \phi), and so is the sound: the demo plays exactly this cosine, sped up 200 times, fading slowly.
Friction fades the note but keeps the rate. Friction shrinks the swing, which is why a note fades, but light friction of the usual kind, proportional to speed, does not make the rate depend on the size of the swing either.



Step-by-step derivationThe motion with friction uses derivatives

Add a friction force proportional to the velocity, -2m\gamma\,\dot x, so that \ddot x = -(k/m) x - 2\gamma\dot x. Then x = a e^{-\gamma t}\cos(\omega_d t + \phi) with \omega_d = \sqrt{k/m - \gamma^2} is a solution, as long as the friction is light (\gamma^2 < k/m); differentiating twice checks it. The swing shrinks, so the motion no longer repeats exactly, but the rate of its swings, \omega_d, still does not depend on a.


Why “barely” sags, not “never”. All of this needs the pull to be exactly proportional to the stretch. Pulled very far, a real spring stops obeying Hooke’s law, and then a bigger swing does change the rate (anharmonicity). A string shows a small version of this: a hard pluck stretches it, raising its tension, so the note starts very slightly sharp and settles as it fades (J. O. Smith, Physical Audio Signal Processing). That is why the pitch barely sags, rather than not at all. For the gentle vibrations of most playing, the linear law holds well.

title: Why does a fading note stay in tune?
text:
What we found
Newton’s law with Hooke’s pull gave the equation m\ddot x = -kx; the operator is the smallest there is, multiply by k/m; its spectrum is that one number, and its square root, divided by 2\pi, is the one frequency, f = \frac{1}{2\pi}\sqrt{k/m}: a single stem, a pure tone. The amplitude is not in it, which is why a fading note keeps its pitch, very nearly. One mass gives one stem on the pitch ruler; a note needs many. On the next page the one number becomes a table of numbers, a matrix, with many eigenvalues, and so many frequencies.

Listen first: an octave tuned to exactly 2 : 1, then a stretched one. The slow wobble in loudness is called a beat.

title: Why do piano tuners stretch octaves?
section: 1 · Newton’s law: the equation of motion
text:
1 · Newton’s law: the equation of motion
Mathematics used: partial derivatives (explained) and the small-angle approximation.
Here is where the piano’s frequencies come from. Apply Newton’s law, mass times acceleration equals force, to one short piece of wire. Two forces act on it, tension and bending, and the piano’s whole story is that they add.
1. One small piece. Follow the stretch of wire between x and x+dx, and let u(x,t) be its height above the rest line at time t; subscripts are partial derivatives. The piece has mass \mu\,dx, where \mu is the mass per unit length, and vertical acceleration u_{tt}, so Newton’s law for its up-and-down motion reads 
\mu\,dx\,u_{tt} = \text{net force on the piece}.

2. Tension pulls a curved piece toward the inside of its curve. The rest of the wire pulls on each end of the piece with the tension T, along the wire.

  
  
  
  
  
  TT
  xx+dx
  T uₓ(x)curved piece, mass μ dx
  T uₓ(x+dx)

At the right end the pull points along the wire, which makes a small angle \theta with the horizontal there. Its upward part is T\sin\theta; for a small angle \sin\theta \approx \tan\theta (both are about \theta in radians), and \tan\theta is the slope u_x(x+dx), so the upward part is T\,u_x(x+dx). At the left end it is -T\,u_x(x). Together, 
T\,\big[u_x(x+dx) - u_x(x)\big] \approx T\,u_{xx}\,dx .
 A straight piece feels no net pull; a curved one is pulled toward the inside of its curve. This is the violin string’s force, unchanged.
3. Bending pushes back too. Steel also resists being bent, exactly like the kalimba’s tine, and the kalimba page derives this force step by step. How sharply the wire bends, its curvature u_{xx}, sets a turning effect inside it, the bending moment EI\,u_{xx}. How that moment changes along the wire sets the sideways force across each cut, the shear force -EI\,u_{xxx}. And how the shear force changes along the wire is the net force on the piece: 
\text{bending force} = -EI\,u_{xxxx}\,dx ,
 where E is steel’s Young’s modulus, how stiff the material is, and I = \pi d^4/64 is the second moment of area of a round wire of diameter d, how strongly its cross-section resists bending.
4. Newton’s law. The two forces simply add: 
\mu\,dx\,u_{tt} = T\,u_{xx}\,dx - EI\,u_{xxxx}\,dx .
 Dividing by \mu\,dx, and writing c^2 = T/\mu and \kappa^2 = EI/\mu, 
u_{tt} = c^2\,u_{xx} - \kappa^2\,u_{xxxx}.

What we assumed. A plain (unwound) steel wire: bass strings are wound with copper, which adds mass but little stiffness. Small slopes; a tension that does not change as the wire flexes; a uniform wire; the spin of each thin slice neglected (Rayleigh’s correction for it adds a small term); and no damping, which the fold in stage 5 adds back.

title: Why do piano tuners stretch octaves?
text:
2 · The operator
Dividing by the mass per unit length puts the equation in the series’ form u_{tt} = -A\,u: the force per unit mass is a fixed rule applied to the wire’s shape, and that rule is the wire’s operator. The ends complete it. The bridge at one end and a metal bearing point at the other hold the wire in place, so u = 0 there. If they let the wire pivot freely they exert no bending moment, and the moment is EI\,u_{xx}, so also u_{xx} = 0. These are called pinned ends. Real piano strings are held a little more firmly than pinned, which shifts the numbers slightly but not the picture.

The piano wire’s operator. The equation of motion is u_{tt} = -A\,u, with 
A = -c^2\frac{d^2}{dx^2} + \kappa^2\frac{d^4}{dx^4},
 where c^2 = T/\mu and \kappa^2 = EI/\mu, acting on shapes with u = u_{xx} = 0 at both ends. The first term is the string’s operator, from tension; the second is the kalimba’s, from bending. A piano wire is both at once: operators add. In words: the force per unit mass on each point is the string’s pull toward the inside of the curve plus the bar’s push back against bending.

title: Why do piano tuners stretch octaves?
text:
3 · Its spectrum
A mode is a shape X that the operator only rescales: A X = \lambda X, with the number \lambda called its eigenvalue. Released in that shape, the wire keeps it and swings as X(x)\cos\omega t, with \omega = \sqrt{\lambda}, so at the frequency f = \sqrt{\lambda}/2\pi. The list of all the eigenvalues is the operator’s spectrum. Here is the wire’s.
1. Try a sine, which already satisfies the pinned ends. Take X = \sin(kx) with k = n\pi/L, where L is the wire’s length and n = 1, 2, 3, \dots It is zero at both ends, and so is X'' = -k^2X: both pinned conditions hold.
2. Apply the operator: each term rescales the same sine. Two derivatives give X'' = -k^2X and four give X'''' = k^4X, so 
A X = \big(c^2k^2 + \kappa^2k^4\big)\,X .
 The sine is rescaled, not reshaped: it is an eigenfunction, with eigenvalue \lambda_n = c^2k^2 + \kappa^2k^4. Each term rescales the same sine, so the string’s eigenvalue and the bar’s simply add. That is special to pinned ends, where the two operators share their eigenfunctions; with clamped ends the formula needs a small correction. There are no other modes: the sines already form a complete set (page 4), and since the operator is symmetric, an eigenfunction for any other eigenvalue would be perpendicular to every sine, hence zero.
3. The frequencies: the string’s, nudged up by stiffness. Factoring out the string’s part, 
\omega_n^2 = \lambda_n = c^2k^2\Big(1 + \frac{EI}{T}\,k^2\Big),
 and with k = n\pi/L, 
\omega_n^2 = \Big(\frac{n\pi c}{L}\Big)^2\Big(1 + \frac{\pi^2EI}{TL^2}\,n^2\Big).
 Taking the square root and dividing by 2\pi gives the result.

The piano wire’s spectrum. Modes \sin(n\pi x/L), n = 1, 2, 3, \dots, with frequencies 
f_n = n f_0\sqrt{1 + Bn^2},
 with eigenvalues \lambda_n = (2\pi f_n)^2 and the stiffness constant B = \pi^2 EI/(T L^2). Here f_0 = c/2L is the lowest frequency the same wire would have without stiffness; the actual fundamental is f_1 = f_0\sqrt{1 + B}. Each partial sits at f_n/f_1 = n\sqrt{(1 + Bn^2)/(1 + B)} times the fundamental: a little above n, more so the larger n.

The stiffness constant B is small, but it multiplies n^2, so the fundamental barely moves while high partials run noticeably sharp: the string is slightly inharmonic.
How big is B? For a middle C wire, roughly d = 1 mm and L = 0.6 m, with steel’s E = 2\times10^{11} Pa and density 7850 kg/m³; a tension of about 610 N then gives middle C. So I \approx 4.9\times10^{-14} m^4 and B \approx 4.4\times10^{-4}. The 10th partial (the fundamental counts as the 1st), at 10f_0\sqrt{1 + 100B}, then sits 1200\log_2\sqrt{(1 + 100B)/(1 + B)} \approx 37 cents sharp of ten times the fundamental, about a third of a semitone. These numbers are rough; real strings vary. Since I grows like the fourth power of the diameter and B falls like 1/L^2, short treble strings, thick for their length, are the stiffest.

title: Why do piano tuners stretch octaves?
text:
4 · On the spectrum diagram
Here are the frequencies of a piano note, middle C, or the last key you played on the keyboard below. Each stem is one f_n/f_1 = n\sqrt{(1 + Bn^2)/(1 + B)} from the result box of stage 3, with that key’s B. They sit a little sharp of the gray lines, and the higher the partial, the further sharp; the readout gives the shift in cents, hundredths of a semitone. The low partials are so close to the lines that the ear still hears one clear note. Each stem’s height is how strongly the hammer starts that mode; the hammer strikes an eighth of the way along, where the 8th and 16th modes stand still, so those two are nearly silent.

title: Why do piano tuners stretch octaves?
text:
5 · What we hear
Why exact octaves beat. A tuner sets an octave by ear, listening for beats between the lower note’s second partial and the upper note’s fundamental. Two nearly equal frequencies played together beat at a rate equal to their difference. The spectrum says where the lower note’s second partial sits: 
\frac{f_2}{f_1} = 2\sqrt{\frac{1 + 4B}{1 + B}} \approx 2\Big(1 + \frac{3B}{2}\Big),
 using \sqrt{1+x} \approx 1 + x/2 (square it: (1 + x/2)^2 = 1 + x + x^2/4, and x^2/4 is tiny) and 1/\sqrt{1+x} \approx 1 - x/2 for small x. So the second partial is more than twice the fundamental, by a factor of about 1 + 3B/2. An upper note tuned to exactly twice the fundamental sits just below it, and the two beat. The tuner raises the upper note until the beat stops, which makes the octave slightly wider than 2 : 1. Tuners also listen to other pairs, such as the lower note’s fourth partial against the upper note’s second, and stiffness makes it impossible to silence all of them at once, so real tuning is a compromise; tick “Play every partial” in the demo at the top to hear it, as the stretched octave then wobbles too. Repeated across the keyboard, this is stretch tuning: compared with equal temperament, the top of a piano ends up sharp and the bottom flat. On a stiff string, “exactly 2 : 1” lines up the wrong pair of frequencies.
A struck wire moves as the sum of its modes, u = \sum_n a_n X_n \cos(2\pi f_n t + \phi_n), so its sound is a sum of tones at the frequencies f_n of stage 3, each fading at its own rate (damping, added to the model); the demos on this page synthesize it exactly this way. Because the low partials sit so close to the lines, the ear hears one clear note.
Hammer, dampers and pedals: none of them moves a frequency. The frequencies belong to the operator, set by the wire’s tension and stiffness. The hammer decides how much of each mode starts, and the felt dampers decide how fast each mode dies. Every control a pianist touches does one of these two things; only the tuner’s wrench, which changes the tension, changes the operator and moves the frequencies. You can try them all on the whole piano further down.



DetailsWhat each control changes

The hammer starts each mode in proportion to the mode’s own height where the hammer hits, so a mode that stands still there stays silent. In a simple model, the felt dampers make each mode die at a rate proportional to how much it moves under the felt. The pedals act on one or the other:

Step-by-step derivationThe full string equation, the hammer weights and the damping rates uses integrals of products of modes and a first-order approximation

The operator is only part of the string’s equation. A real string is also pushed by the hammer and loses energy to damping; here f(x,t) is a force, not a frequency: 
\mu\,u_{tt} + b(x,t)\,u_t = T\,u_{xx} - EI\,u_{xxxx} + f(x,t).

Each term has one job. The operator’s term, T\,u_{xx} - EI\,u_{xxxx} (that is, -\mu A u), fixes the frequencies and the mode shapes. The forcing f is the hammer, and it fixes how much of each mode is excited. The damping b is the felt dampers plus small internal losses, and it fixes how fast each mode dies. Every control a pianist touches acts on f or on b. Only the tuner’s wrench, which changes T, touches the operator.
Both effects are read off the mode shapes X_n(x) = \sin(n\pi x/L). A hammer blow at x_h gives mode n a weight proportional to X_n(x_h), the mode’s own height at the hammer. The drum on the next page uses the same rule. A damper felt resting on a short stretch W of the string makes mode n’s swing shrink like e^{-\gamma_n t}, and for weak damping (to first order in b, that is, ignoring terms in b^2) the decay rate is 
\gamma_n = \frac{\int_W b\,X_n^2\,dx}{2\mu\int_0^L X_n^2\,dx}.
 A mode is damped in proportion to how much it moves under the felt, and its frequency shifts only by an amount proportional to \gamma_n^2, negligible for weak damping. A mode with a node under the felt barely notices the damper: in the view of the inside of the piano further down, slide the damper to L/8, where the hammer also sits, and the 8th mode, which has a still point there, is not excited and barely damped.
In the table above, the dampers and the sustain pedal change b; the soft pedal and the practice mute change f; only the tuning pin changes the operator.
1. Expand in modes. Write u(x,t) = \sum_n q_n(t)\,X_n(x), with A X_n = \omega_n^2X_n and the pinned conditions.
2. Project. Substitute into the full equation, multiply by X_m and integrate along the string. The operator is symmetric with these boundary conditions (in fact self-adjoint), by integrating by parts as on the circle page, so the X_n are orthogonal: \int_0^L X_mX_n\,dx = 0 for m \ne n. The acceleration and operator terms collapse to one term each: 
\mu N_m\,(\ddot q_m + \omega_m^2 q_m) + \sum_n D_{mn}\,\dot q_n = F_m(t),
 with N_m = \int X_m^2\,dx, D_{mn} = \int b\,X_mX_n\,dx and F_m = \int f\,X_m\,dx.
3. The hammer. The felt touches a short stretch near x_h, so F_m(t) \approx X_m(x_h)\,P(t), where P(t) is the total force. Every mode gets the same push in time, weighted by X_m(x_h): the mode’s own height at the hammer.
4. The damper. If the damping is weak, the cross terms D_{mn} with m \ne n change the answer only at second order. Keeping the diagonal leaves a damped oscillator for each mode, 
\ddot q_m + 2\gamma_m\,\dot q_m + \omega_m^2 q_m = 0, \qquad \gamma_m = \frac{D_{mm}}{2\mu N_m},
 whose solution e^{-\gamma_m t}\cos\big(\sqrt{\omega_m^2 - \gamma_m^2}\,t\big) decays at the rate \gamma_m while its frequency moves only by order \gamma_m^2/\omega_m.
5. Honest limits. A real damper is not weak: it stops a note in a fraction of a second. The formula gives the right picture, that modes are damped by how much they move under the felt, but not exact decay times.

title: Why do piano tuners stretch octaves?
text:
What we found
Newton’s law on a short piece of wire (stage 1) gave its operator (stage 2), A = -c^2\,d^2/dx^2 + \kappa^2\,d^4/dx^4: the string’s operator plus the bar’s. Operators add, and with pinned ends so do their eigenvalues, so the spectrum is f_n = n f_0\sqrt{1 + Bn^2} (stage 3). That puts every partial a little sharp of the lines of the spectrum diagram (stage 4), more so the higher it goes: close enough that you hear one clear note, far enough that an exact octave beats, which is why tuners stretch (stage 5). The hammer, the dampers and the pedals act on how the modes start and die, not on the operator, so none of them moves a frequency by more than a hair.

Every real string is a little stiff. Guitar and harp strings belong here too, faintly. The piano is where stiffness is large enough to hear, and large enough to change how pianos are tuned.

DetailsWhere the dampers sit: under-damper and birdcage uprights

Where the dampers touch the string matters, because each mode is damped in proportion to its motion under the felt. Close to an end every low mode barely moves, so a damper there hardly damps the bass. In most modern uprights the dampers sit below the hammers, nearer the middle of the string; in older “birdcage” uprights they sat above the hammers, near the end. Piano restorers report that the under-damper design stops the strings better, partly because its dampers are closer to the middle of the string (Sykes). The slider in the view above moves the damper and shows the effect on each mode.





Reader questionWhat does a damper do, and what would a piano without dampers sound like?

Without dampers, releasing a key would do nothing: every string would ring until it died on its own, exactly as if the sustain pedal were always down. On a real piano each key lifts a felt damper off its strings; letting go drops the damper back and stops the note within a fraction of a second. The sustain pedal lifts all the dampers at once, so released notes keep ringing. The keyboard above models both. The top 20 keys have no dampers at all, as on a real piano: those short strings die out quickly by themselves.

title: The Shape of a Sound
text: Pluck a string and you get a note you could hum. Strike a drum and you get a thud. Both are a stretched piece of material, set shaking. So why do they sound so different?

title: The Shape of a Sound
text:
The answer in three steps
1. Everything that vibrates has a set of favorite shapes. A string can swing as one arc, as two halves moving in opposite directions, as three thirds, and so on. Each of these shapes, called a mode, swings at its own frequency.
1×2×3×
2. A pluck sets many of them going at once. What you hear is a chord of the modes’ frequencies: the lowest, called the fundamental, and the overtones above it. They are the stems on the ruler above.
3. Whether that chord sounds like one note depends on how the frequencies line up. If they sit at, or very near, whole-number multiples of one frequency in the range we hear as pitch, the sound repeats itself many times a second, and the ear hears that repetition rate as the pitch. A string’s modes do exactly that: 1×, 2×, 3×, …. An ideal drumhead’s land at 1×, 1.59×, 2.14×, 2.30×, …: a few fall near a line by chance, but no frequency we hear as pitch fits them all. The sound doesn’t repeat at any rate we hear as pitch, and it dies fast: a thud.

The idea behind the whole series. Newton’s law turns each instrument into an operator, and the operator’s spectrum gives its frequencies: how the instrument is built, stretched and held decides them. Put the frequencies you hear on the pitch ruler: on the lines, a note; off the lines, a clang or a thud. More exactly, you hear a note when they all sit at, or very near, whole-number multiples of one frequency in the range we hear as pitch. Each instrument page puts its instrument on the ruler to see which.

title: The Shape of a Sound
section: The mathematics: one recipe, every instrument
text:
The mathematics: one recipe, every instrument
Behind every page is the same recipe, and it is the mathematical heart of the series: Newton’s law gives each instrument an operator, and the operator’s spectrum gives its frequencies. The page The spectrum of an operator lays the idea out in full and runs it on every instrument; here are its two steps.
1. Derive the instrument’s operator from first principles. Take one small piece of the instrument (a bit of string, a slab of air, a slice of steel, a patch of drumhead) and apply Newton’s law: mass times acceleration equals the force on it. The force comes from the material: tension, air pressure, or the stiffness of bent steel. Worked out, the force on the piece turns out to depend only on the shape of the instrument around it, through a fixed rule. Dividing by the mass gives an equation of the same form for every instrument, 
u_{tt} = -A\,u ,
 where u is the instrument’s shape (how far each point is from rest; for a tube, the air pressure), u_{tt} is its acceleration, and A is the operator: the rule that takes a shape and returns minus the restoring force per unit mass. How the instrument is held (ends tied, clamped, open, free) decides which shapes A may act on, and is part of the operator.
2. Find its spectrum. A mode is a shape that the operator only rescales, 
A\,X = \lambda\,X ,
 for some number \lambda, an eigenvalue. Every operator here has \lambda \ge 0 (where \lambda = 0 occurs, it is the whole instrument drifting, which makes no sound). For \lambda > 0 such a shape swings in place as X\cos(\sqrt{\lambda}\,t + \phi), so it sounds at the frequency 
f = \frac{\sqrt{\lambda}}{2\pi} .
 The list of all the eigenvalues is the operator’s spectrum. So the frequencies an instrument rings at on its own, once struck or plucked, are fixed by its operator; how you strike or pluck it only decides how strongly each one sounds. A steady bow or breath can do more: it can lock the sound onto exact whole-number multiples (pages 4, 5 and 6b).

A clear pitch means the frequencies you hear sit at, or very near, whole-number multiples of one frequency in the pitch range, from a few dozen to a few thousand hertz. title: Why is a clarinet almost an octave deeper than a flute?
section: 1 · Newton’s law: the equation of motion
text:
1 · Newton’s law: the equation of motion
Mathematics used: partial derivatives, including mixed ones (explained).
The air in a tube is a long column of tiny slabs, each pushed back and forth by the pressure on its two faces. We apply Newton’s law, mass times acceleration equals force, to one slab, and combine it with the way air pushes back when it is squeezed.

  
  
  
  
  p(x)p(x+dx)
  slab, mass ρS dx

1. How far the air moves. Let \xi(x, t) be how far the air that normally sits at x has moved along the tube, and let the tube’s cross-section have area S. Let p(x, t) be the air pressure in the tube minus room pressure. Subscripts are partial derivatives: \xi_t is the rate of change in time with x held fixed, \xi_x the rate of change along the tube with t held fixed.
2. A pressure difference pushes the slab. The slab of air between x and x + dx has mass \rho S\,dx, where \rho is the density of air. The only force on it along the tube is the pressure difference between its two faces, S\,[p(x) - p(x + dx)] \approx -S\,p_x\,dx. Mass times acceleration equals force, divided by S\,dx: 
\rho\,\xi_{tt} = -p_x .

3. Squeezed air pushes back. The slab’s two faces move by \xi(x) and \xi(x + dx), so its length changes by \xi(x + dx) - \xi(x) \approx \xi_x\,dx: it is stretched by the fraction \xi_x, and its pressure drops in proportion, 
p = -K\,\xi_x ,
 where K is the bulk modulus, air’s resistance to being squeezed (this K has nothing to do with the bead matrix of page 2). In a sound wave the squeezing is too fast for heat to flow, which is called adiabatic; for air this makes K about 1.4 times atmospheric pressure.
4. A pressure slope pushes the air, and moving air changes the pressure: together they make a wave. To combine steps 2 and 3, differentiate both. A mixed subscript means differentiating more than once in turn: \xi_{ttx} means twice in t, then once in x. For a smooth motion the order does not matter, so \xi_{xtt} = \xi_{ttx}. Differentiate step 2 once in x: 
\rho\,\xi_{ttx} = -p_{xx} .
 Differentiate step 3 twice in t: p_{tt} = -K\,\xi_{xtt} = -K\,\xi_{ttx}. Put in \xi_{ttx} = -p_{xx}/\rho from the line above, and \xi is gone: 
p_{tt} = \frac{K}{\rho}\,p_{xx} .
 It is the string’s wave equation again, with pressure in place of sideways displacement and c = \sqrt{K/\rho}, the speed of sound, about 343 m/s at 20 °C, in place of the string’s wave speed.
What we assumed. The tube is a cylinder, narrow compared with the sound’s wavelength, so the pressure is the same across it; the pressure changes are small; friction with the walls is left out. A real clarinet’s bore is not exactly cylindrical, and its holes and bell matter; they refine the numbers below, not the picture.

title: Why is a clarinet almost an octave deeper than a flute?
text:
2 · The operator
Read the equation as a rule: the pressure’s rate of change, twice over in time, is c^2 times its curvature along the tube. So the operator is the string’s, A = -c^2\,d^2/dx^2, now acting on pressure shapes, and the equation reads p_{tt} = -A\,p. What differs between a flute and a clarinet is only which shapes the operator may act on: the ends.
The ends. At an open end the air in the tube meets the room, so the pressure there is room pressure: p = 0. This is approximate: the air just outside moves with the air inside, so the tube acts as if it were slightly longer, by about 0.6 of its radius at each open end, an amount called the end correction. At the clarinet’s reed the opening is nearly shut, so the air there cannot move back and forth. Air that never moves has no acceleration, so by step 2 the pressure has no slope there: p_x = 0. The air piles up and thins out against the closed end, and the pressure swings most there. The first condition is the string’s Dirichlet condition; the second, a condition on the slope, is called a Neumann condition.

The tube’s operator. 
\begin{gathered}
p_{tt} = -A\,p, \qquad A = -c^2\,\frac{d^2}{dx^2}, \\
c^2 = \frac{K}{\rho} \approx (343\ \text{m/s})^2,
\end{gathered}
 acting on pressure shapes along a tube of length L. Flute, open at both ends: p(0) = p(L) = 0. Clarinet, closed at the reed (x = 0) and open at the bell: p_x(0) = 0 and p(L) = 0. In words: the same rule as the string, with different ends.

title: Why is a clarinet almost an octave deeper than a flute?
text:
3 · Its spectrum
A mode is a pressure shape X(x) that the operator only rescales, A X = \lambda X; it swings at the frequency f = \sqrt\lambda/2\pi, and the list of all the eigenvalues is the spectrum. The ends decide which shapes are allowed.
1. Which shapes does the operator only rescale? Writing \lambda = c^2k^2, the mode equation -c^2X'' = \lambda X becomes X'' = -k^2X, solved by the waves 
X = a\cos kx + b\sin kx, \qquad f = \frac{\sqrt\lambda}{2\pi} = \frac{ck}{2\pi} .

2. The flute: room pressure at both ends. X(0) = 0 forces a = 0, and X(L) = 0 needs \sin kL = 0, so kL = n\pi: one half wave, two half waves, and so on. The eigenvalues are \lambda_n = (n\pi c/L)^2 and the frequencies f_n = n\,c/2L.
3. The clarinet: no pressure slope at the reed, room pressure at the bell. X'(0) = bk = 0 at the reed forces b = 0, leaving X = \cos kx, and X(L) = 0 at the open end needs \cos kL = 0, so kL = (2n - 1)\pi/2: one quarter wave, three quarter waves, and so on. The eigenvalues are \lambda_n = \big((2n-1)\pi c/2L\big)^2 and the frequencies f_n = (2n-1)\,c/4L.

The two spectra.
Flute, open at both ends: modes \sin(n\pi x/L), eigenvalues (n\pi c/L)^2, frequencies f_n = n\,c/2L, that is 1, 2, 3, 4, … times the lowest.
Clarinet, closed at the reed and open at the bell: modes \cos\big((2n-1)\pi x/2L\big), eigenvalues \big((2n-1)\pi c/2L\big)^2, frequencies f_n = (2n-1)\,c/4L, that is 1, 3, 5, 7, … times the lowest.
The lowest frequencies are c/2L and c/4L: a ratio of exactly 2 for the same ideal tube.




ProofAnother way to see the odd multiples: the closed tube is a quarter of a loop uses the circle’s eigenfunctions (page 3)

Use the reflections from the string page. Take a pressure shape p on [0, L] with p_x(0) = 0 and p(L) = 0.

Reflect it evenly across the reed end, p(-x) = p(x). A smooth even shape has zero slope at 0, so even reflection is what the Neumann condition p_x(0) = 0 allows, so the result is a shape on [-L, L] that vanishes at both ends.
Reflect that oddly across x = L, p(2L - x) = -p(x), and repeat. The result is a shape on a loop of circumference 4L.
On that loop the eigenfunctions are \cos(k\pi x/2L) and \sin(k\pi x/2L). Step 1 keeps only cosines. Step 2 needs \cos\big(k\pi(2L - x)/2L\big) = (-1)^k\cos(k\pi x/2L) to equal -\cos(k\pi x/2L), which keeps only odd k.

So the clarinet’s modes are the odd multiples of a loop four tube-lengths long, which is where both the factor 4 and the odd numbers come from.

The flute’s stems sit on every line. title: Why is a clarinet almost an octave deeper than a flute?
text:
5 · What we hear
Almost an octave deeper. The flute’s lowest mode, \sin(\pi x/L), has room pressure at both ends and swings most in the middle: half a wavelength fits in the tube. The clarinet’s, \cos(\pi x/2L), swings most at the reed and has room pressure at the open end: only a quarter of a wavelength fits. A wave twice as long has half the frequency, so the same ideal tube sounds exactly an octave lower closed at one end. Real flutes and clarinets differ a little in length, the clarinet’s mouthpiece and bell change its effective length, and the open ends act slightly longer than they are, so the real interval comes out a bit less than an octave.
A blown tube does not ring and fade like a plucked string: the reed or the air jet keeps feeding it, and the air settles into one motion that repeats, at a frequency close to the tube’s sounding mode from stage 3. The demo’s sound is made that way: a repeating wave at that mode’s frequency, with the strong odd multiples and faint even ones described below.
Overblowing: an octave or a twelfth. The flute’s spectrum has every whole-number multiple of its lowest frequency; the clarinet’s has only the odd ones, with nothing in between. So when a clarinetist presses the register key, the tube jumps to its next mode, 3 times its lowest frequency, an octave and a fifth, called a twelfth (a fifth is the ratio 3/2). (The demo keeps the low-register tone color when the register key is on.) A flutist overblows by blowing harder, and the flute’s next mode is 2 times its lowest, an octave. That is why clarinet fingerings repeat a twelfth apart and flute fingerings an octave apart.



DetailsHow the register key picks out the 3× mode

The clarinet’s register key opens a small hole near the top of the tube. An open hole lets air in and out, pulling the pressure there toward room pressure, which spoils the fundamental, a mode that needs pressure variation at that point. For one note in the lower part of the low register (the notes played without the key), the hole sits about a third of the way down the sounding tube, right where that note’s 3f_1 mode has no pressure variation anyway, so the open hole does not disturb that mode (Wolfe). For the other notes the hole is off that point, well off for the lowest and highest notes you play with the key (Wolfe), and a second effect helps: the air in a small hole has mass, and the faster it must move back and forth, the harder it is to move. At the fundamental’s lower frequency it moves more easily, so the hole leaks enough to spoil that mode; at the higher frequency of the 3f_1 mode it moves much less, so the hole acts almost as a plug. Either way the tube jumps to the 3f_1 mode.


Why the sound still lands on every line. The reed is a valve: when the pressure in the mouthpiece drops it closes, and when the pressure rises it opens, so the air column drives the reed that feeds it. In normal playing this settles into a periodic oscillation, a sound that repeats, at a playing frequency close to the tube’s lowest mode. A sound that repeats has frequencies only at whole-number multiples of its repetition rate (page 0), but it may have all of them. So the tube’s modes are odd multiples only, while the clarinet’s sound has even multiples too: weak in the low register (the lowest notes), where no mode of the tube supports them, but not absent.

title: Why is a clarinet almost an octave deeper than a flute?
text:
What we found
Newton’s law on a slab of air, together with air’s resistance to being squeezed, gave the wave equation for the pressure. Read as a rule, it is the string’s operator, A = -c^2\,d^2/dx^2, acting on pressure; only the ends differ. With room pressure at both ends, the flute’s spectrum gives frequencies n\,c/2L: every whole-number multiple. With the air held still at the reed, the clarinet’s gives (2n-1)\,c/4L: half the lowest frequency and only odd multiples. On the diagram both blown sounds sit on the lines, because they repeat; what we hear is the octave between them, and the twelfth a clarinet jumps when overblown.

Same operator, other ends. Stopped organ pipes and pan pipes are closed at one end like the clarinet and share its odd-multiples spectrum. Open organ pipes share the flute’s. Oboes and saxophones have cone-shaped tubes instead of cylinders, a different operator, which this series does not cover.

title: How can a tangled wobble be a few simple motions?
section: 1 · Newton’s law: the equation of motion
text:
1 · Newton’s law: the equation of motion
Mathematics used: the small-angle approximation and multiplying a table of numbers by a list (explained).
As on page 1, apply Newton’s law to one piece of the instrument, here one bead, and find the force. It will turn out to depend on the bead’s neighbors as well as on the bead itself.
Let u_j be the height of bead j, with N beads, each of mass m, spaced h apart along a string of tension T. Because the loop closes, bead N is next to bead 1, so bead numbers are counted around the ring. (An idealization: the model keeps only the sideways pulls between neighbors, as for a straight string whose two ends are joined.)

  
  
  
  
  
  bead j−1bead jbead j+1
  TTnet pull

1. The string on one side pulls the bead toward its neighbor. The string between beads j and j+1 pulls bead j along itself with force T. That piece of string rises by u_{j+1} - u_j over a distance h, so its slope is (u_{j+1} - u_j)/h. If the string makes a small angle \theta with the horizontal, the upward part of the pull is T\sin\theta; for a small angle \sin\theta \approx \tan\theta (both are about \theta in radians), and \tan\theta is the slope. So the vertical part of the pull is 
T\sin\theta \approx T\tan\theta = \frac{T}{h}\,(u_{j+1} - u_j) .

2. The string on the other side does the same. Its vertical part is 
\frac{T}{h}\,(u_{j-1} - u_j) .

3. The two pulls set the bead’s acceleration. Adding them and setting the total equal to mass times acceleration, 
m\,\ddot u_j = \frac{T}{h}\left(u_{j+1} - 2u_j + u_{j-1}\right).
 The bracket is twice the gap between the average of the two neighbors and bead j itself: a bead sitting above its neighbors is pulled down, one sitting below is pulled up. So each bead is a mass on a spring, except that where its spring pulls it depends on where its neighbors are.
What we assumed. Small slopes, a tension that does not change as the string flexes, point-like beads on a massless string, no friction, and the idealized closed ring described above.

title: How can a tangled wobble be a few simple motions?
text:
2 · The operator
The force on each bead depends on its neighbors, so the rule that turns the shape into the force acts on all the beads at once. Collect the heights into one column u = (u_1, \dots, u_N). The N equations become one, 
\ddot u = -\frac{T}{mh}\,K\,u ,
 where K is a square table of numbers, a matrix, with 2 down its diagonal (top left to bottom right), -1 just above and below it, and -1 in the two corners, because bead 1 and bead N are neighbors. For N = 5, 
K = \begin{pmatrix} 2 & -1 & 0 & 0 & -1\\ -1 & 2 & -1 & 0 & 0\\ 0 & -1 & 2 & -1 & 0\\ 0 & 0 & -1 & 2 & -1\\ -1 & 0 & 0 & -1 & 2 \end{pmatrix}.
 Here Ku is the column whose j-th entry is row j of K times u: multiply each entry of row j by the matching entry of u, and add. Row j has 2 in place j and -1 in places j - 1 and j + 1, so (Ku)_j = 2u_j - u_{j-1} - u_{j+1}, which is the bead equation for every bead at once. Each row of K is the row above shifted one place to the right, wrapping around; a matrix with this property is called circulant. The two corner entries are the ring’s boundary condition: they are where the loop closes.

The operator. 
\ddot u = -A\,u, \qquad A = \frac{T}{mh}\,K ,
 a matrix acting on the list of all the beads’ heights, with the ring closed (bead N next to bead 1). In words: on page 1 the operator was one number; here it is a table of numbers, and A\,u is the list of restoring forces per unit mass, reversed.

title: How can a tangled wobble be a few simple motions?
text:
3 · Its spectrum
A mode is a shape that keeps its form while it swings. Most starting shapes change as they move: that is the tangle. But in a few special shapes, every bead is pulled back in proportion to its own height, by the same factor for every bead. Then every bead is a mass on the same spring, they all swing in step, and the shape only grows and shrinks. In matrix language, a nonzero column v is an eigenvector of A, with eigenvalue \lambda, if 
A v = \lambda\, v ,
 so the matrix only rescales it, possibly by zero. The list of all the eigenvalues is the matrix’s spectrum. Since A = \frac{T}{mh}K, the eigenvectors of A are those of K: if Kv = s\,v, then Av = \lambda v with \lambda = \frac{T}{mh}\,s. So it is enough to find the eigenvectors of the simpler matrix K.
1. Each eigenvector swings like one mass on a spring. If Av = \lambda v, try u(t) = v\cos(\omega t). Differentiating twice gives \ddot u = -\omega^2 v\cos\omega t, while -Au = -\lambda\, v\cos\omega t. These agree when 
\omega^2 = \lambda .
 Every bead swings at the same angular frequency \omega = \sqrt{\lambda} (radians per second; page 1), in the fixed shape v: the mass on a spring again, once for each eigenvector, at frequency f = \sqrt{\lambda}/2\pi.
2. With three beads, find the special shapes by hand. For N = 3, 
K = \begin{pmatrix} 2 & -1 & -1\\ -1 & 2 & -1\\ -1 & -1 & 2 \end{pmatrix}.
 Row j gives (Kv)_j = 3v_j - (v_1 + v_2 + v_3). The column (1, 1, 1) gives K(1,1,1) = (0,0,0): an eigenvector with s = 0. Every bead moves up together, nothing stretches, nothing pulls back, and the frequency is 0, so the ring just drifts; this is the mode 0 of the demo. Any column whose entries add up to zero gives (Kv)_j = 3v_j, so Kv = 3v. Every such column is a combination a(1, -1, 0) + b(0, 1, -1), so these eigenvectors fill a whole plane: every one is built from those two shapes, and neither of the two is a multiple of the other. The eigenvalues of K are 0, 3, 3, with 3 counted twice: it has multiplicity 2. Those of A are 0 and 3T/mh, twice.
3. For any number of beads, the special shapes are waves around the ring. On a ring no bead is special, so try waves that fit a whole number of times around: v_j = \cos(2\pi jk/N), a wave with k crests. The identity \cos(a + b) + \cos(a - b) = 2\cos a\cos b, with a = 2\pi jk/N and b = 2\pi k/N, gives v_{j+1} + v_{j-1} = 2\cos(2\pi k/N)\,v_j, so 
\begin{aligned}
(Kv)_j &= 2v_j - v_{j+1} - v_{j-1} \\
&= \big(2 - 2\cos(2\pi k/N)\big)\,v_j \\
&= 4\sin^2\!\Big(\frac{\pi k}{N}\Big)\,v_j ,
\end{aligned}
 using 1 - \cos 2x = 2\sin^2 x. The same holds for v_j = \sin(2\pi jk/N). These are the shapes the mode buttons play. At the beads, a wave with N - k crests looks exactly like one with k crests (the cosine is the same and the sine changes sign), so the different eigenvalues come from k = 0, 1, \dots up to N/2, rounded down, and each one from k = 1 up to just below N/2 has two eigenvectors, a cosine and a sine. (At k = 0, and at k = N/2 when N is even, the sine is zero at every bead, so only the cosine is left.) A wave with more crests bends more sharply from bead to bead, so each bead is pulled back harder and the wave swings faster.

The spectrum. Eigenvectors: the waves \cos(2\pi jk/N) and \sin(2\pi jk/N) with k crests. Eigenvalues of A: 
\lambda_k = \frac{4T}{mh}\,\sin^2\!\Big(\frac{\pi k}{N}\Big), \qquad f_k = \frac{\sqrt{\lambda_k}}{2\pi} = \frac{1}{\pi}\sqrt{\frac{T}{mh}}\,\sin\frac{\pi k}{N} .
 In words: mode k sounds at \sin(\pi k/N)/\sin(\pi/N) times mode 1.

In the 1730s Daniel Bernoulli studied systems like this, weights strung along a flexible thread and a hanging chain, and came to believe that every vibration is built from such simple motions; in 1753 he put this forward as a general principle. For the beads it is a theorem, and writing a motion as a sum of these waves is the discrete Fourier transform.



ProofEvery motion is a sum of modes uses linear algebra

The matrix A is symmetric: the entry in row i, column j equals the entry in row j, column i. By the spectral theorem for symmetric matrices, A has a basis of N mutually orthogonal (perpendicular) eigenvectors v^{(1)}, \dots, v^{(N)} with real eigenvalues \lambda_1, \dots, \lambda_N. Write the motion as u(t) = \sum_k a_k(t)\,v^{(k)}. Substituting into \ddot u = -Au and taking the dot product with v^{(k)}, which removes every other term because they are perpendicular, gives \ddot a_k = -\lambda_k a_k: each coefficient obeys its own mass-on-a-spring equation, with \omega_k = \sqrt{\lambda_k}. With starting shape u(0) = \sum_k c_k v^{(k)} and starting velocity \dot u(0) = \sum_k d_k v^{(k)}, and by the uniqueness of solutions from page 1, every motion is u(t) = \sum_k \big(c_k\cos\omega_k t + \frac{d_k}{\omega_k}\sin\omega_k t\big)v^{(k)}, read as c_k + d_k t when \omega_k = 0. The eigenvalues are nonnegative because u \cdot Ku = \sum_j u_j(2u_j - u_{j+1} - u_{j-1}) = \sum_j (u_{j+1} - u_j)^2 \ge 0, by regrouping the terms around the ring; for an eigenvector of A this gives \lambda\,(u\cdot u) = \frac{T}{mh}\,u\cdot Ku \ge 0.





PreciselyThe same waves, written with complex numbers uses complex numbers

With Euler’s formula e^{ix} = \cos x + i\sin x, the cosine and sine waves combine into v_j = e^{2\pi i jk/N} for k = 0, 1, \dots, N - 1 (here i is the imaginary unit and j the bead number). Then (Kv)_j = \big(2 - e^{2\pi ik/N} - e^{-2\pi ik/N}\big)v_j = 4\sin^2(\pi k/N)\,v_j in one line. These N waves are the basis vectors of the discrete Fourier transform, and they are eigenvectors of every circulant matrix, not only this one. Combined with the time factor e^{\mp i\omega t}, the waves with k and N - k crests travel around the ring in opposite directions.

title: How can a tangled wobble be a few simple motions?
text:
4 · On the spectrum diagram
The stems are the frequencies f_k from the result box, as multiples of mode 1’s, the slowest wave that swings back and forth: mode k stands at \sin(\pi k/N)/\sin(\pi/N). In the demo at the top, each stem’s height is how much of that mode the current motion contains; below, every mode is drawn equally tall. Apart from mode 1 itself, they generally miss the lines. With 8 beads, as the demo starts, the modes sit at 1×, 1.85×, 2.41× and 2.61×. Raise the number of beads and the low stems close in on the lines: with 24 beads, modes 2 and 3 are within 2.5% of 2× and 3×. The high modes stay far off.


  
  
  Each mode's frequency as a multiple of mode 1's, every mode drawn equally tall: 8 beads (top), 24 beads (bottom). Adding beads pulls the low modes onto the lines; the high ones stay off.

title: How can a tangled wobble be a few simple motions?
text:
5 · What we hear
The jangle is a chord. Pluck one bead and the starting shape is not a wave; but it is a sum of waves, and each wave swings at its own frequency. So the plucked ring sounds all those frequencies at once. They sit off the lines, so the chord is a jangle. Start the ring in one wave’s shape and only that one frequency sounds: a pure tone. The clean tones were in the jangle all along, as its eigenvectors.
Any motion of the ring is a sum of modes, u(t) = \sum_k a_k\, v^{(k)}\cos(2\pi f_k t + \phi_k), each swinging at its own frequency as if it were alone (the proof is in the fold above). The demo’s sound is exactly this sum: it adds the modes’ frequencies f_k, with mode 1 set to 196 Hz, each as strong as the motion contains it.
Almost whole numbers. A long wave, with few crests, spreads over many beads, and to it the beads look like a smooth string; its frequency grows in step with its number of crests, almost exactly as whole numbers do. A short wave, with crests only a bead or two apart, feels the gaps between the beads, and its frequency falls behind. That is why the low stems sit near the lines and close in as you add beads, while the high ones stay off.



PreciselyHow near to whole numbers uses the sine function

Mode k has frequency proportional to \sin(\pi k/N), which is not proportional to k: the beads are not exactly harmonic. For small k, \sin(\pi k/N) \approx \pi k/N, so the low modes are nearly harmonic, and the ratio \sin(\pi k/N)/\sin(\pi/N) tends to k as N grows. The modes near k = N/2 stay far from the whole-number grid: for an even number of beads the largest ratio is 1/\sin(\pi/N) (slightly less for an odd number), and for any number of beads it is about N/\pi once there are many, not N/2. A mode can land on a line by coincidence: with 6 beads, the top mode sits at exactly 2×.

title: How can a tangled wobble be a few simple motions?
text:
What we found
Newton’s law for each bead gave the equation m\ddot u_j = \frac{T}{h}(u_{j+1} - 2u_j + u_{j-1}); written for all the beads at once, it reads \ddot u = -Au with the operator A = \frac{T}{mh}K, a matrix whose corner entries close the ring. Its eigenvectors are waves around the ring, its eigenvalues are \lambda_k = \frac{4T}{mh}\sin^2(\pi k/N), and their square roots, divided by 2\pi, are the modes’ frequencies. On the spectrum diagram the low modes sit near the lines but not on them. Any motion, even a tangle, is a sum of modes: the jangle you hear is that chord, and each clean tone is one eigenvector.
