title: Can you hear the shape of a drum?
text:
← 8 Drum · The Shape of a Sound · Spectrum of an operator · Map · 10 Scales →
Listen first: play each drum with every mode equally loud. Then click a drum to strike it at a point, and compare.

title: Can you hear the shape of a drum?
section: 1 · Newton’s law: the equation of motion
text:
1 · Newton’s law: the equation of motion
Mathematics used: the Laplacian (page 8), and counting.
This page asks what the spectrum says about the drum. First, the equation, which page 8 derived step by step.
Let the drumhead be a region \Omega of the plane, in one piece, and let u(x, y, t) be the height of the head above the point (x, y) at time t. On page 8, Newton’s law for one small patch of the head, pulled by the tension in its edges, gave the drum’s equation 
u_{tt} = c^2\,\Delta u \ \text{ inside } \Omega, \qquad u = 0 \ \text{ on the rim},
 where \Delta u = u_{xx} + u_{yy} is the Laplacian, and c^2 is the tension divided by the mass per unit area. The Laplacian is positive where u at a point sits below the average of u around it, and negative where it sits above; the bigger the gap, the bigger the Laplacian. So the equation says: each point of the head accelerates toward the average height around it.
What we assumed is listed on page 8: small slopes, a tension that is the same everywhere and does not change as the head moves, no bending stiffness, no air, and no damping.

title: Can you hear the shape of a drum?
text:
2 · The operator
In the series’ form u_{tt} = -A\,u, the operator is A = -c^2\Delta, acting on shapes that are zero on the rim. The rim condition is part of the operator: the same rule on a different shape is a different operator.

The drum’s operator: A = -c^2\Delta on the drumhead \Omega, acting on shapes with u = 0 on the rim.
In words: the force per unit mass pulling each point of the head back toward rest is c^2 times how far that point sits from the average around it.

title: Can you hear the shape of a drum?
text:
3 · Its spectrum
When is there a mode? A mode is a shape X that the operator only rescales, A X = \lambda X, with \lambda the eigenvalue. Write \lambda = c^2 k^2, so that the shape must satisfy 
-\Delta X = k^2 X \ \text{ inside } \Omega, \qquad X = 0 \ \text{ on the rim}.
 The numbers k^2 for which this has a solution other than X = 0 are the eigenvalues of -\Delta on \Omega, and the solutions X are its eigenfunctions, the mode shapes. They depend only on the shape \Omega; the factor c^2 only scales them.
List them. Put the eigenvalues in order, k_1^2 \le k_2^2 \le k_3^2 \le \cdots, each repeated as many times as it occurs (its multiplicity). The mode with k_n^2 has the operator’s eigenvalue \lambda_n = c^2k_n^2 and swings at 
f_n = \frac{\sqrt{\lambda_n}}{2\pi} = \frac{c\,k_n}{2\pi}.


The drum’s spectrum: the eigenvalues \lambda_n = c^2k_n^2 of A, where -\Delta X_n = k_n^2 X_n inside \Omega and X_n = 0 on the rim, listed \lambda_1 \le \lambda_2 \le \cdots with repeats. The frequencies are f_n = \sqrt{\lambda_n}/2\pi = c\,k_n/2\pi.
In words: apart from the one overall factor c, the frequencies are decided by the shape of \Omega alone.

Kac’s question, precisely. Suppose we know c, so that hearing every frequency means knowing every k_n^2. Does the list k_1^2, k_2^2, k_3^2, \dots determine \Omega? It can only do so up to sliding, turning or flipping the drum, which changes no frequency. (Kac wrote that he had first heard the question posed this way about ten years earlier, from Salomon Bochner.)

title: Can you hear the shape of a drum?
text:
4 · On the spectrum diagram
Here are both drums’ first twelve frequencies, as multiples of the lowest, \sqrt{\lambda_n/\lambda_1} = k_n/k_1: 1×, 1.20×, 1.43×, 1.60×, 1.69×, 1.90×, 2.04×, …. Like the drum on page 8, they sit off the gray whole-number lines, so neither drum has a clear pitch. And the two lists are the same to every digit computed: the stems under drum A and drum B stand in the same places. In the demo, each stem’s height is how strongly a strike at the clicked point starts that mode (below, every mode is drawn equally tall): all equal until you click, then different on the two drums, because it depends on the mode’s shape at the struck point.


  
  Both drums' first twelve frequencies, as multiples of the lowest, every mode drawn equally tall: drum A and drum B have exactly these stems (Driscoll's values).

title: Can you hear the shape of a drum?
text:
5 · What we hear
Same frequencies, not the same sound. A struck drum moves as a sum of its modes, 
u = \sum_n a_n X_n \cos(2\pi f_n t + \phi_n),
 so its sound is a sum of tones at the frequencies f_n, each fading at its own rate, with a strength a_n that depends on where it is struck; what you hear also depends on where you listen. The demo’s sound is made exactly this way, from the frequencies in stage 3. The two drums share the frequencies f_n. The mode shapes X_n differ, so the strengths from a strike at a given point differ, and so does the timbre, the color of the sound. Played with every mode equally loud, every a_n = 1, the two drums sound identical. What the drums share is the answer to “which frequencies can this drum make”, which is exactly what the spectrum records.

title: Can you hear the shape of a drum?
text:
What the spectrum knows
Counting the frequencies: area and rim. Count the eigenvalues of -\Delta up to a limit \Lambda: 
N(\Lambda) = \#\{n : k_n^2 \le \Lambda\},
 where \# means “the number of”. (A frequency limit f corresponds to \Lambda = (2\pi f/c)^2, since f_n = c\,k_n/2\pi.) For a high limit, 
N(\Lambda) \approx \frac{|\Omega|}{4\pi}\,\Lambda \;-\; \frac{P}{4\pi}\sqrt{\Lambda},
 where |\Omega| is the drum’s area and P the length of its rim. In words: the number of modes below a high limit grows in proportion to the area, so twice the area gives about twice as many modes; and it falls short of the area’s share by an amount in proportion to the rim’s length, because holding the rim still costs the drum some modes.
The first term is Weyl’s law. Hermann Weyl proved it in 1911, and later work extended it to every drum. So the area can be heard: it is 4\pi times the rate at which N(\Lambda) grows. The second term is subtler. For the count itself it is proved only for some drums: Victor Ivrii proved it in 1980 for smooth rims on which closed billiard paths are rare (fold below). For a slightly smoothed version of the count it is proved for every drum whose rim is smooth or made of straight pieces, and that is enough to hear the rim’s length. Where the second term holds, “\approx” means that the error, divided by \sqrt\Lambda, shrinks to zero as \Lambda grows.
The demo counts the modes of three drums with the same area. Once the area’s share, the same for all three, is taken away, the drum with the longest rim sits lowest.


  
  
    Modes below the limit
    Minus the area's share
  
  Frequency limit
  
  Three drums of equal area: a disk, a square, a long rectangle. Steps: the true counts. Dashed: Weyl's formula, area and rim together. Gray: the area's share alone, the same for all three.





PreciselyWhat the demo plots, and Ivrii’s condition on billiard paths uses limits

In the demo all three drums have area |\Omega| = \pi (a disk of radius 1, a square, and a rectangle 4 times as long as it is wide), so the area’s share is \Lambda/4, and “minus the area’s share” plots N(\Lambda) - \Lambda/4, roughly -P\sqrt\Lambda/4\pi: the longer the rim, the lower the curve. The demo’s frequency limit is shown as a multiple of the disk’s lowest frequency, \sqrt{\Lambda}/k_1.
Ivrii’s condition: a billiard path is the path of a ball rolling inside the drum and bouncing off the rim, angle in equal to angle out; it is closed if it comes back to where it started, heading the same way. “Rare” means that if you pick a starting point and a direction at random, the chance of landing on a closed path is zero. Ivrii conjectured that this always holds; it has not been proved. The square and the rectangle in the demo have corners, which his theorem does not cover, but for them the formula can be checked by counting, as in the next fold. The perimeter can be heard in any case, for every drum whose rim is smooth or a polygon, by a smoother way of counting; that is the fold after it.





Proof sketchWeyl’s law for a square, by counting dots uses partial derivatives

Take the square of side s. Its eigenfunctions of -\Delta are \sin(m\pi x/s)\sin(n\pi y/s) for whole numbers m, n \ge 1, with eigenvalues k^2 = (\pi/s)^2(m^2 + n^2); substituting them into the equation checks this, as for the circle on page 3. So N(\Lambda) is the number of dots (m, n), with m, n \ge 1, inside the quarter circle of radius R = s\sqrt\Lambda/\pi.















RR

Give each dot the unit square centered on it. These squares nearly fill the quarter disk, which has area \pi R^2/4. What they miss is a strip of width \tfrac12 along each axis, of area about R/2 each, shaded in the figure; the squares sticking out past the arc and the gaps inside it roughly cancel. So 
N(\Lambda) \approx \frac{\pi R^2}{4} - R = \frac{s^2}{4\pi}\Lambda - \frac{4s}{4\pi}\sqrt\Lambda = \frac{|\Omega|}{4\pi}\Lambda - \frac{P}{4\pi}\sqrt\Lambda .
 In the figure, R = 5.3: there are 17 dots, and the formula gives 16.8. The strips are missing because m = 0 and n = 0 give the zero function, not an eigenfunction: the rim’s condition u = 0 is what costs the perimeter term. Making “roughly cancel” precise is a classical problem about counting lattice points in a circle.





Proof sketchHearing the perimeter of any drum: a smoother count uses the heat equation and the reflection trick of page 4

N(\Lambda) jumps by one at every eigenvalue, and those jumps can bunch up, which is what Ivrii’s condition controls. A smoother count avoids them. For t > 0 let 
Z(t) = \sum_n e^{-k_n^2 t}.
 Each eigenvalue adds nearly 1 if k_n^2 is much less than 1/t and nearly 0 if it is much more, so Z(t) is roughly N(1/t), with the jumps smoothed out. Like N, Z is determined by the list of eigenvalues.
Z has a physical meaning. Heat spreading on the drumhead, with the rim held at temperature 0, obeys v_t = \Delta v, the drum’s equation with one time derivative instead of two, so each mode now decays like e^{-k_n^2 t} instead of oscillating. Start a unit burst of heat at a point x and let it spread for time t. The temperature it leaves at x itself, added up over all points x of the drum, is Z(t). (Write the burst as a sum of modes, each scaled so that \iint X_n^2\,dA = 1. A burst at x contains mode n in proportion to X_n(x), the same rule as a strike on the drum page; after time t that part has shrunk by e^{-k_n^2 t}, and its temperature at x is again proportional to X_n(x). So the temperature left at x is \sum_n e^{-k_n^2 t}X_n(x)^2, and adding it up over the drum gives \sum_n e^{-k_n^2 t}.) In a short time t heat travels a distance of about \sqrt t, so a burst only feels the rim if it starts within about that distance of it. Kac called this “not feeling the boundary”. Then:

Away from the rim, the burst spreads as on an endless plane, and the temperature it leaves at its starting point is 1/(4\pi t). Adding this up over the drum gives |\Omega|/(4\pi t).
Near a straight piece of rim, at distance r from it, the rim’s condition v = 0 is met by adding a mirror-image burst of opposite sign on the far side of the rim, the odd reflection of the string page. The image is a distance 2r away, and lowers the temperature at x by e^{-r^2/t}/(4\pi t). Adding this up over a strip along the rim, using \int_0^\infty e^{-r^2/t}\,dr = \tfrac12\sqrt{\pi t} for each unit of rim length, gives -P/(8\sqrt{\pi t}).

So, as t \to 0, 
Z(t) = \frac{|\Omega|}{4\pi t} - \frac{P}{8\sqrt{\pi t}} + (\text{terms that stay bounded}).
 Knowing Z, one reads off |\Omega| from the first term and then P from the second. Kac gave this argument in his 1966 paper. Åke Pleijel had already proved the formula for smooth rims in 1954, by another method; Henry McKean and Isadore Singer proved in 1967 the next, constant term, which Kac had conjectured, from an argument that was not a full proof: (1 - h)/6 for a drum with h holes and a smooth rim; and Michiel van den Berg and Sivakolundu Srisatkunarajah proved the formula for polygons in 1988. Unlike N, Z needs no condition on billiard paths, because averaging over a range of eigenvalues smooths out the bunching.


So a round drum can be heard. Of all shapes with the same area, the disk has the shortest rim. This is the isoperimetric inequality: every drum satisfies 
P^2 \ge 4\pi\,|\Omega|,
 with equality only for the disk. Both sides can be heard, for a rim that is smooth or made of straight pieces. So a drum with such a rim that has exactly a disk’s frequencies has the disk’s area and rim length, so P^2 = 4\pi|\Omega|, so it is a disk. Kac pointed this out in section 10 of his 1966 paper: “By pitch alone one can thus determine whether a drum is circular or not!”
But in general, no. Two years before Kac’s paper, John Milnor had found two different shapes with the same frequencies, and Kac said so; but they were 16-dimensional and had no rim. (They are flat tori: 16-dimensional versions of a video-game screen whose edges wrap around, so that leaving on the right brings you back on the left.) For drums in the plane the question stayed open for 26 years. In 1992 Carolyn Gordon, David Webb and Scott Wolpert answered it: no. They found two different polygons with exactly the same frequencies, repeats included: the two drums at the top of this page. Such drums are called isospectral. Since area and rim length can be heard, they must share them, and they do: each is made of seven copies of the same right triangle, with two short sides of length 1, so each has area 3.5 and rim length 6 + 3\sqrt2.
Why do they share every frequency? Cut each drum into its seven triangles. Any mode of drum A can be rebuilt on drum B: fill each of B’s triangles with three triangle-shaped pieces of the mode, taken from A’s triangles, turned or flipped to fit, some with their signs reversed. With the right choice of pieces and signs, they join smoothly across every seam and stay still on B’s rim, so the result is a mode of B, at the same frequency. The construction runs backwards too, so the two drums have exactly the same frequencies, with the same number of modes at each.



DetailsTransplantation: carrying a mode from one drum to the other uses the Laplacian (page 8)

Cut each drum along its seams into its seven triangles. Take any eigenfunction X of drum A, with -\Delta X = k^2 X. On each triangle of drum B, place a sum of three pieces of X, each taken from one of A’s triangles, turned or reflected to fit, and some with a minus sign. Each piece satisfies -\Delta X = k^2 X, so the sum does too, inside each triangle. With the right choice of pieces and signs, the result is zero on B’s rim, and across every seam of B both its values and its slopes match. A function that satisfies the equation on both sides of a line, with values and slopes matching on the line, satisfies it across the line too, a standard fact about this equation. At the points where several seams meet, one more standard fact closes the gap: a solution that stays bounded around a single point, and satisfies the equation everywhere near it except possibly at the point itself, satisfies it there too. So the result is an eigenfunction of B with the same k^2, and so the same frequency. The construction can be reversed, so each eigenvalue has the same multiplicity on both drums.
This argument is called transplantation. It grew out of work of Peter Buser on surfaces in the 1980s and of Pierre Bérard around 1992; the version for drums like these is in a 1994 paper of Buser, John Conway, Peter Doyle and Klaus-Dieter Semmler. The seven formulas, with pictures, are in Cleve Moler’s blog post on transplantation, and in S. J. Chapman’s article, which does the same by folding paper. Gordon, Webb and Wolpert’s own proof used a method of Toshikazu Sunada from 1985 for building isospectral spaces from group theory; Wikipedia has an overview.





DetailsHow the numbers on this page were computed uses matrices, as on page 2

Each drum is covered by a square grid of spacing h, and the Laplacian is replaced by its five-point version: at each grid point, the sum of the four neighbors minus four times the point, divided by h^2. This is the bead model of page 2 in two dimensions. Grid points on the rim are held at zero. The drums’ corners sit on grid points, so whether each point is inside, on the rim, or outside is decided with exact whole-number arithmetic.
At h = 1/40 and h = 1/80 the two drums give the same first twelve eigenvalues k_n^2 of -\Delta to a relative difference of 3\times10^{-14}, which is rounding error. This is expected, as far as I can tell, because the grid lines up with every triangle’s edges, so transplantation works for the grid model too; Moler’s post transplants grid eigenvectors in the same way. Combining the two grids (Richardson extrapolation) gives values within 0.03% of the high-accuracy values in Table 3.1 of Driscoll’s paper, after multiplying his by 4: his drums are twice the size of these. That is a check, not a precise computation: Richardson’s trick assumes the grid error shrinks like h^2, and the drums’ inward-pointing corners slow that down. The page uses Driscoll’s values.
One eigenvalue is known exactly, the ninth, k_9^2. Its mode is, on each triangle, that triangle’s own lowest mode, \sin\pi x\,\sin 2\pi y - \sin 2\pi x\,\sin\pi y in coordinates where the triangle has corners (0,0), (1,0) and (1,1), with its sign flipping across each seam. Substituting gives k_9^2 = \pi^2(1 + 4) = 5\pi^2 = 49.348\ldots, and Driscoll’s value agrees to every digit he gives. On the grid, the ninth eigenvalue equals the grid version of this mode’s eigenvalue to rounding error, a second check.
The scripts are gww.py for the eigenvalues and gww_modes.py for the mode pictures. The corner coordinates are those in Moler’s first post. The mode pictures use the coarser grid h = 1/40, sampled every 0.1.

title: Can you hear the shape of a drum?
text:
What we found
Run forwards, the recipe gives the drum’s sound: Newton’s law on a patch of head gives u_{tt} = c^2\Delta u; the operator is A = -c^2\Delta with the rim held still; its spectrum is the list of eigenvalues \lambda_n = c^2k_n^2, with -\Delta X_n = k_n^2X_n, and the frequencies are f_n = \sqrt{\lambda_n}/2\pi. Run backwards, it asks what the spectrum says about the drum. Counting the spectrum with Weyl’s law recovers the drum’s area and, for smooth or straight-sided rims, the length of its rim, and for a round drum that pins down the shape. In general it does not: two differently shaped drums can share every eigenvalue, and so every frequency, though struck at a point they still sound different. On the spectrum diagram, both drums are off the lines, like the ideal drumhead of page 8, and in exactly the same places. The study of such questions, what a spectrum says about the shape behind it, is called spectral geometry.

title: The spectrum of an operator
text:
1 · What an operator is
Mathematics used on this page: derivatives, partial derivatives and integration by parts.
The same pattern appears three times on pages 1 to 3, each time on a bigger object.
One mass on a spring (page 1). The spring pulls back with force -kx, so Newton’s law reads m\ddot x = -kx, that is 
\ddot x = -A\,x, \qquad A = \text{multiply by } \frac{k}{m} .
 Here A acts on a single number, the displacement.
Beads on a ring (page 2). Each bead of mass m is pulled by the string toward its two neighbors, a distance h away, with force \frac{T}{h}(u_{j+1} - 2u_j + u_{j-1}) for small motions. All the beads at once: 
\ddot u = -A\,u, \qquad A = \frac{T}{mh}\,K ,
 where u is the list of all the beads’ heights and K is a square table of numbers, a matrix, with 2 down its diagonal, -1 beside it, and -1 in the two corners, where the ring closes. Here A acts on a list.
A string (pages 3 and 4). In the limit of many beads, the pull on each bit of string is tension times curvature, and Newton’s law becomes the wave equation 
u_{tt} = c^2\,u_{xx}, \qquad\text{that is}\qquad u_{tt} = -A\,u, \quad A = -c^2\,\frac{d^2}{dx^2}, \quad c^2 = \frac{T}{\mu} .
 Here u(x, t) is the height of the string at position x and time t, subscripts are partial derivatives, and A acts on a whole shape, a function of x.

Definition. For a vibrating object, the operator A is the rule that takes a shape of the object (how far each point is from rest; for a tube, the air pressure) and returns minus the acceleration it causes at every point (for a string or a bar, minus the restoring force per unit mass). It acts only on the shapes allowed by how the object is held. Newton’s law then reads 
u_{tt} = -A\,u .
 In words: the acceleration of every point is the restoring force on it, per unit mass.

Why does every instrument come out this way? Because for small motions every restoring force in the series is proportional to the shape: tension pulls a curved string back in proportion to its curvature, squeezed air pushes back in proportion to the squeeze, bent steel pushes back through the change of its bending. Double the shape and the force doubles; add two shapes and their forces add. So A is linear: A(au + bv) = a\,Au + b\,Av for numbers a, b. That is all the next sections use. (Larger motions break this, and with it the recipe; see page 1 on amplitude.)

title: The spectrum of an operator
text:
2 · Why a mode swings at √λ / 2π
A mode is a shape that the operator only rescales, 
A\,X = \lambda\,X ,
 for some number \lambda, an eigenvalue of A; the shape X is an eigenfunction (for the beads, an eigenvector). The list of all the eigenvalues, each counted as many times as it has modes (its multiplicity), is the operator’s spectrum. Here is why each eigenvalue is a frequency.

Start the object in the shape of a mode and let go. Try a motion that keeps that shape and only changes its size: u(x, t) = X(x)\,q(t), with AX = \lambda X.
Newton’s law for this motion. The left side is u_{tt} = X\,q''. The right side is -Au = -q\,AX = -\lambda\,q\,X, since A is linear and q(t) is just a number at each moment. So X\,q'' = -\lambda\,q\,X, and dividing by X, 
q'' = -\lambda\,q .

This is page 1’s spring. For \lambda > 0 its solutions are q(t) = \cos(\sqrt{\lambda}\,t + \phi), times any number: the shape swings with angular frequency \omega = \sqrt{\lambda}. For \lambda = 0 the solutions are q = a + bt: the whole object drifting, with no sound. A negative \lambda would give exponential growth; section 3 shows it never happens.


Eigenvalues are frequencies. A mode with eigenvalue \lambda > 0 swings in place at 
f = \frac{\sqrt{\lambda}}{2\pi} .
 In words: \lambda is restoring force per unit mass per unit displacement, a stiffness over a mass, and the frequency goes as its square root, as for a mass on a spring.

title: The spectrum of an operator
section: 3 · Why every motion is a chord
text:
3 · Why every motion is a chord
Modes alone would be a curiosity if the object could also move in other ways. It cannot: every motion is a sum of modes, each at its own frequency. Three facts about A make this so. They all come from one identity.
The identity: the operator is symmetric. Measure how much two shapes f and g overlap by 
\langle f, g\rangle = \int_0^L f(x)\,g(x)\,dx
 (for the beads, \sum_j f_j g_j; for a drum, an integral over the head). For the string, integrate by parts once: 
\langle Af, g\rangle = -c^2\int_0^L f''\,g\,dx = -c^2\big[f'\,g\big]_0^L + c^2\int_0^L f'\,g'\,dx .
 If the ends are tied, g(0) = g(L) = 0 and the bracket vanishes. (It also vanishes on a loop, where the two ends are the same point, and at a closed tube end, where f' = 0.) What is left, c^2\int f'g'\,dx, does not change when f and g swap places. So 
\langle Af, g\rangle = \langle f, Ag\rangle .
 This is what it means for A to be symmetric. For a kalimba tine, integrating by parts twice gives \kappa^2\int f''g''\,dx, with every boundary term killed by the clamped and free ends; for a drum, the two-dimensional version gives c^2\iint \nabla f\cdot\nabla g\,dA (here \nabla f = (f_x, f_y), the slope in each direction, and \nabla f\cdot\nabla g = f_x g_x + f_y g_y), with the rim term killed by the fixed rim. The same holds for every instrument in the series: each way of holding an instrument that appears here makes the boundary terms vanish.
Fact 1: modes with different frequencies are perpendicular. If AX = \lambda X and AY = \mu Y, then \lambda\langle X, Y\rangle = \langle AX, Y\rangle = \langle X, AY\rangle = \mu\langle X, Y\rangle. If \lambda \neq \mu, this forces \langle X, Y\rangle = 0: the two shapes do not overlap at all, in the sense above. (Modes that share an eigenvalue, like a loop’s cosine and sine, can be chosen perpendicular too.)
Fact 2: no eigenvalue is negative. Put g = f in the identity: \langle Af, f\rangle = c^2\int (f')^2\,dx \ge 0. For a mode, \lambda\langle X, X\rangle = \langle AX, X\rangle \ge 0, so \lambda \ge 0. The physics is energy. Let 
E(t) = \tfrac12\langle u_t, u_t\rangle + \tfrac12\langle Au, u\rangle .
 Times the mass per unit length, the first term is the kinetic energy and the second the energy stored in the stretched string (\tfrac12 T\int u_x^2\,dx). Using symmetry, E' = \langle u_t, u_{tt}\rangle + \langle Au, u_t\rangle = \langle u_t, u_{tt} + Au\rangle = 0 by Newton’s law: energy is conserved, and since the stored part can never be negative, no mode can grow exponentially (a mode with \lambda = 0 can only drift). For the string, zero occurs only for a shape with no slope anywhere, the whole string moving at once, which a tied end forbids. (For a bar with both ends free, the zero modes are the bar sliding and tilting as a whole.)
Fact 3: the modes are complete. Every allowed shape f is a sum of modes, f = \sum_n a_n X_n, and Fact 1 gives the amounts: taking the overlap of both sides with X_m kills every term but one, so 
a_n = \frac{\langle f, X_n\rangle}{\langle X_n, X_n\rangle} .
 For the beads this is the spectral theorem for symmetric matrices, used on page 2. For strings, tubes, bars and drums it is a theorem of analysis (fold below); on the loop it is Fourier’s theorem, page 3.



PreciselyCompleteness for differential operators uses functional analysis

Work in the space L^2 of shapes with finite \int f^2, with the overlap above as inner product. On its natural domain (shapes with enough derivatives and the boundary conditions), each operator in the series is self-adjoint, not merely symmetric, and non-negative. Its inverse, or (A + 1)^{-1} where 0 is an eigenvalue (the loop, free ends), is a compact operator: for one-dimensional objects it is an integral operator with a continuous kernel, the Green’s function; for a drum on a bounded region this is Rellich’s theorem. The spectral theorem for compact self-adjoint operators then gives an orthonormal basis of L^2 made of eigenfunctions, with eigenvalues \lambda_1 \le \lambda_2 \le \cdots \to \infty, each of finite multiplicity. For one-dimensional problems this is Sturm–Liouville theory; Courant and Hilbert, volume 1, chapters V and VI, treat all the cases in this series. The series converges in the L^2 sense; for one-dimensional problems and smooth shapes satisfying the boundary conditions it also converges uniformly.


Now put the three facts together. Start the object in any shape u(x, 0) = f(x) with any velocity u_t(x, 0) = g(x), and expand both in modes, f = \sum a_n X_n and g = \sum b_n X_n. Each term X_n(x)\cos(\omega_n t) and X_n(x)\sin(\omega_n t) obeys Newton’s law by section 2, and since A is linear, so does any sum of them. The sum 
u(x, t) = \sum_n X_n(x)\Big(a_n\cos\omega_n t + \frac{b_n}{\omega_n}\sin\omega_n t\Big), \qquad \omega_n = \sqrt{\lambda_n},
 matches the starting shape and velocity, so it is the motion (two motions with the same start differ by one that starts flat and at rest; its energy is 0 and stays 0, so they are the same). (A mode with \lambda_n = 0 contributes a_n + b_n t instead: drifting, no sound.)

Every motion is a chord. Whatever you do to the instrument, its free motion is a sum of its modes, each swinging at its own frequency f_n = \sqrt{\lambda_n}/2\pi. The spectrum fixes the frequencies; the start (how and where you pluck or strike) fixes only the amounts a_n and b_n.

section: 4 · How the instrument is held is part of the operator
text:
4 · How the instrument is held is part of the operator
The rule alone is not the operator: the allowed shapes are part of it. Take the same rule, -c^2\,d^2/dx^2, on a piece of length L, and hold the ends in three ways. Writing X as a sine or cosine of kx, so that AX = c^2k^2X, each way of holding picks out different values of k:









Held
Modes
Eigenvalues \lambda_n
Frequencies f_n




as a loop: X(x + L) = X(x)
\cos\frac{2\pi n x}{L}, \sin\frac{2\pi n x}{L}
\big(\frac{2\pi n c}{L}\big)^2
\frac{nc}{L}: 0, 1, 2, 3, \dots


both ends tied (string; flute, on pressure): X(0) = X(L) = 0
\sin\frac{n\pi x}{L}
\big(\frac{n\pi c}{L}\big)^2
\frac{nc}{2L}: 1, 2, 3, \dots


one end closed (clarinet, on pressure): X'(0) = 0, X(L) = 0
\cos\frac{(2n-1)\pi x}{2L}
\big(\frac{(2n-1)\pi c}{2L}\big)^2
\frac{(2n-1)c}{4L}: 1, 3, 5, \dots



(On the loop each n \ge 1 has two modes, the cosine and the sine; page 3 uses a loop of length 2\pi, where f_n = nc/2\pi.) The same happens for a bar, where the rule is \kappa^2\,d^4/dx^4: clamped at one end and free at the other (kalimba, harmonica reed), the frequencies stand in the ratios 1 : 6.27 : 17.55; pinned at both ends, 1 : 4 : 9; free at both ends (glockenspiel), 1 : 2.76 : 5.40. Change how the instrument is held and you change its spectrum, without touching the physics of the material.

title: The spectrum of an operator
section: 5 · From the spectrum to the sound
text:
5 · From the spectrum to the sound
The spectrum gives the frequencies. Three more things decide what reaches your ear.
How you play sets the heights. The amounts a_n, b_n come from the starting shape and velocity, so where and how you pluck or strike decides which modes start and how strongly. A string plucked a fifth of the way along starts no 5th mode, because that mode stands still at the pluck point (page 4); a drum struck at its center starts only the round modes (page 8). On the spectrum diagram, the stems stand at the frequencies the spectrum gives, and their heights are set by the playing.
Each mode fades at its own rate. Real instruments lose energy to friction, to the air and to their supports. For light losses each mode still swings at very nearly its own frequency, and its size fades away (page 1, and the piano’s dampers on page 7). So the sound is 
p(t) \approx \sum_n c_n\, e^{-t/\tau_n}\cos(2\pi f_n t + \phi_n),
 with the frequencies f_n from the spectrum and amounts and fading times c_n, \tau_n from the playing, the losses and the way the instrument passes its motion to the air. That passing on is linear too (a violin’s body, for instance), so it changes the heights of the stems, never their positions (page 4). Every plucked or struck sound in this series’ demos is made exactly this way: a sum of sine waves at the frequencies from the spectrum, each fading at its own rate. The bowed and blown sounds (pages 4, 5 and 6b) are made differently: a wave repeating at the playing frequency, so their frequencies are its whole-number multiples (apart from the violin’s gentle vibrato and the chromatic harmonica’s breath noise). The frequencies come from the operator; the amounts and fading times are modelling choices, rough values chosen to illustrate.
Then the ear. If the frequencies you hear sit at, or very near, whole-number multiples of one frequency in the range we hear as pitch, you hear a note (page 0).
What the operator does not decide, the series also shows. A kalimba’s off-line overtones fade within a fraction of a second, so what you hear is mostly one frequency (page 6). And a steady bow or breath is not a free vibration at all: it keeps feeding energy in, and the motion locks into one exactly repeating pattern near one of the modes’ frequencies, usually the lowest (observed, not derived in this series), so the sound sits exactly on the lines even when the operator’s other frequencies do not (the violin, page 4; the clarinet’s sound, page 5; the harmonica, page 6b).

title: The spectrum of an operator
text:
6 · The recipe on every instrument
Each card runs one instrument through the same five stages as its own page, in compact form; the link at the bottom leads to the page with every step derived. The stems show the spectrum on the spectrum diagram, as multiples of the lowest frequency; the button plays the sound made from it.


A mass on a spring
▶ Playa pure tone

Newton’s law on the mass, with the spring pulling back with force -kx (Hooke’s law): m\ddot x = -kx.
The operator: A multiplies by k/m; there is nothing to hold.
Its spectrum: one eigenvalue, \lambda = k/m, so one frequency, f = \sqrt{k/m}\,/2\pi.
On the diagram: a single stem.
What you hear: a pure tone, at the same pitch however far you pull the mass, as long as the pull stays proportional to the stretch.

Every step on page 1 →


Beads on a ring
▶ Play8 beads, every mode equally strong

Newton’s law on each bead, pulled toward its two neighbors by the string’s tension T: m\,\ddot u_j = \frac{T}{h}\,(u_{j+1} - 2u_j + u_{j-1}), the beads numbered around the ring.
The operator: A = \frac{T}{mh}K, a matrix acting on the list of heights; held as a ring, so bead N + 1 is bead 1.
Its spectrum: the modes are waves \cos\frac{2\pi jk}{N} and \sin\frac{2\pi jk}{N} that fit k times around the ring, with \lambda_k = \frac{4T}{mh}\sin^2\frac{\pi k}{N}, so f_k = \frac{1}{\pi}\sqrt{\frac{T}{mh}}\,\sin\frac{\pi k}{N}.
On the diagram: for 8 beads, stems at 1, 1.85, 2.41 and 2.61 times the lowest; the low ones near the lines, the high ones well below.
What you hear: one bead plucked, a jangle of all the modes; started in a single mode, one clean tone.

Every step on page 2 →


A loop of string
▶ Playevery stem on a line

Newton’s law on a short bit of string, where tension pulls along the string so the net pull is tension times curvature: u_{tt} = c^2\,u_{\theta\theta}, with c^2 = T/\mu, around a loop of length 2\pi.
The operator: A = -c^2\,d^2/d\theta^2, on shapes that close up, X(\theta + 2\pi) = X(\theta).
Its spectrum: \cos n\theta and \sin n\theta close up only for whole numbers n, so \lambda_n = c^2 n^2, each n \ge 1 twice, and f_n = nc/2\pi.
On the diagram: every stem exactly on a line, 1 : 2 : 3 : \cdots.
What you hear: a sound that repeats every 1/f_1 seconds, a note at f_1.

Every step on page 3 →


A violin string
▶ Playplucked a fifth of the way along

Newton’s law on a short piece of string under tension T, where for small slopes the upward part of each end’s pull is tension times slope: u_{tt} = c^2\,u_{xx}, with c^2 = T/\mu.
The operator: A = -c^2\,d^2/dx^2, with both ends tied, u(0) = u(L) = 0.
Its spectrum: X = \sin kx with \sin kL = 0, so k = n\pi/L, \lambda_n = (n\pi c/L)^2 and f_n = \frac{n}{2L}\sqrt{T/\mu}.
On the diagram: every stem on a line; plucked a fifth of the way along, the 5th is missing.
What you hear: a clear note at f_1; a light touch at the middle keeps only the even modes, an octave up.

Every step on page 4 →


A flute and a clarinet
▶ Flute▶ Clarinetthe tubes' spectra; blown, the clarinet's sound also has faint even multiples

Newton’s law on a thin slab of air, pushed by a pressure difference, \rho\,\xi_{tt} = -p_x, with squeezed air pushing back, p = -K\xi_x, gives p_{tt} = c^2\,p_{xx}, with c^2 = K/\rho, for the pressure p.
The operator: A = -c^2\,d^2/dx^2, on pressure shapes. Flute, open at both ends: p(0) = p(L) = 0. Clarinet, closed at the reed: p_x(0) = 0, p(L) = 0.
Its spectrum: flute, \sin kL = 0, so f_n = nc/2L; clarinet, \cos kL = 0, so f_n = (2n-1)c/4L.
On the diagram: the flute’s stems on every line, the clarinet’s on the odd lines only, 1 : 3 : 5 : \cdots.
What you hear: two notes, the clarinet’s almost an octave lower for the same length; blown, its sound also has faint even multiples (page 5).

Every step on page 5 →


A kalimba tine
▶ Playthe overtones fade almost at once

Newton’s law on a thin slice of steel, where bending stretches one side and squeezes the other, giving a bending moment M = EI\,u_{xx} and a shear force V = -M_x: \rho S\,u_{tt} = -EI\,u_{xxxx}.
The operator: A = \kappa^2\,d^4/dx^4, with \kappa^2 = EI/\rho S; clamped at the bridge (u = u_x = 0), free at the tip (u_{xx} = u_{xxx} = 0).
Its spectrum: \cos\beta L\,\cosh\beta L = -1, with \lambda = \kappa^2\beta^4, so f_n = \kappa\beta_n^2/2\pi with \beta_nL = 1.875, 4.694, 7.855, \dots.
On the diagram: stems at 1, 6.27 and 17.55 times the lowest, off the lines.
What you hear: off the lines, but the overtone dies within a fraction of a second: a brief click, then a clean note.

Every step on page 6 →


A harmonica reed
▶ Plucked▶ Blownsame reed, two ways of playing

Newton’s law: the kalimba tine’s, for a small brass bar riveted at one end.
The operator: the tine’s, with \kappa^2 = Eh^2/12\rho for thickness h.
Its spectrum: the same ratios, 1 : 6.27 : 17.55, with f_1 = \frac{(1.8751)^2}{2\pi}\,\frac{h}{L^2}\sqrt{\frac{E}{12\rho}}.
On the diagram: plucked, off the lines like the tine; blown, every stem on a line.
What you hear: plucked, this spectrum; blown, the reed chops the airflow into puffs that repeat exactly, and the sound sits at whole-number multiples of the puff rate.

Every step on page 6b →


A piano wire
▶ Playstiffness exaggerated (B = 0.0012)

Newton’s law on a short piece of stiff wire, where tension pulls it straight and the steel resists bending, the two forces adding: u_{tt} = c^2\,u_{xx} - \kappa^2\,u_{xxxx}, with c^2 = T/\mu, \kappa^2 = EI/\mu.
The operator: A = -c^2\,d^2/dx^2 + \kappa^2\,d^4/dx^4, with the ends pinned, u = u_{xx} = 0.
Its spectrum: X = \sin kx with \sin kL = 0 and \lambda = c^2k^2 + \kappa^2k^4, so f_n = n f_0\sqrt{1 + Bn^2}, with f_0 = c/2L and B = \pi^2 EI/TL^2.
On the diagram: each stem a little sharp of its line, more so the higher it is.
What you hear: still a clear note, but an octave tuned to exactly 2 : 1 beats, so tuners stretch octaves.

Every step on page 7 →


A drum
▶ Playstruck about a third of the way out

Newton’s law on a small patch of drumhead, where tension T pulls all around the patch’s edge and the divergence theorem turns the total pull into T\,\Delta u per unit area: \sigma\,u_{tt} = T\,\Delta u, with \Delta u = u_{xx} + u_{yy}, the Laplacian.
The operator: A = -c^2\,\Delta, with c^2 = T/\sigma, and the rim held fixed, u = 0.
Its spectrum: for a round drum of radius a, J_m(ka) = 0 (Bessel functions), with \lambda = c^2k^2, so f_{m,n} = c\,j_{m,n}/2\pi a.
On the diagram: stems at 1, 1.59, 2.14, 2.30, 2.65, 2.92, … times the lowest, scattered between the lines.
What you hear: a sound that doesn’t repeat at any rate we hear as pitch, and that fades fast: a thud (an ideal head; timpani differ, page 8).

Every step on page 8 →

The last two pages turn the recipe around. Page 9 asks how much of a drum’s shape its spectrum determines, and page 10 asks whether the spectra of instruments shaped the scales we play on them.

title: The spectrum of an operator
text:
What we found
One recipe explains every instrument in the series. Newton’s law on a small piece gives an equation of motion of the form u_{tt} = -A\,u; the operator A, a rule together with the way the instrument is held, is linear and symmetric; its eigenvalues are never negative, and each one, \lambda, is a mode swinging at f = \sqrt{\lambda}/2\pi; and every motion is a sum of these modes. So the spectrum of the operator fixes where the stems of the spectrum diagram stand, plucking or striking fixes their heights (a steady bow or breath can do more), and the ear hears a note when the stems sit on, or very near, the lines of the pitch ruler.

References. N. H. Fletcher and T. D. Rossing, The Physics of Musical Instruments, 2nd ed., Springer, 1998, chapters 1–3. R. Courant and D. Hilbert, Methods of Mathematical Physics, vol. 1, Interscience, 1953, chapters V and VI. The instrument-specific facts quoted here (the kalimba’s fast-fading overtone, the clarinet’s faint even multiples, the harmonica’s puffs, the glockenspiel’s free bar) are sourced on their own pages. title: How to Break Nested For Loop
text: Using a few examples, we demonstrate how to conditionally break out of nested for loop using for-else clause.

title: How to Break Nested For Loop
How to Break Nested For Loop
text:
2 Double Nested for Loop
Here, the program halts right after (i,j) reaches (2,1), which is what we want.

for i in range(4): # Layer 1
    print(f"Layer 1 for i = {i}: start")
    for j in range(3): # Layer 2
        print(f"  {i} {j}")
        if (i, j) == (2, 1):
            break
    else: # reached <=> for loop layer 2 was broken
        print(f"  Layer 2 for i = {i}: finished")
        continue # continuing for the enclosing for loop (layer 1), thus ignoring the "break"
    break # reached <=> continue was not called <=> for loop layer 2 was broken

Layer 1 for i = 0: start
  0 0
  0 1
  0 2
  Layer 2 for i = 0: finished
Layer 1 for i = 1: start
  1 0
  1 1
  1 2
  Layer 2 for i = 1: finished
Layer 1 for i = 2: start
  2 0
  2 1


Here, no continue in the else part. Thus, the program breaks unconditionally after finishing its job in the i==0 round.

for i in range(4):
    print(f"Layer 1 for i = {i}: start")
    for j in range(3):
        print(f"  {i} {j}")
        if (i, j) == (2, 1):
            break
    else: # reached <=> the for loop layer 2 was broken
        print(f"  Layer 2 for i = {i}: completed")
    break # always reached at i = 0

  0 0
  0 1
  0 2
  Layer 2 for i = 0: completed

3 Triple Nested for Loop
OK, we’ve learnt enough. Now, let’s test it on a triple nested for loop!

            if (i,j,k) == (1,2,0):
                break
        else:
            continue
        break

    break
